studyMetadata.title: Grow in Christ (volume 1)
studyMetadata.subtitle: Discipleship course
studyMetadata.description: Are you growing in Christ? God wants all his children to grow in Jesus. If you are not growing, these studies will help you work out what is wrong and how to put it right. If you are growing, they will help you grow more. Working through Scripture, each session combines close reading with personal reflection.
studyMetadata.author: Rick Creighton

theme.theme-annotation: Green study theme — muted sage and forest palette. Organic and grounded, evoking growth, new life, and the natural world. Suited to studies on renewal, creation, or spiritual formation. Restful rather than urgent.

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup>’The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe the gospel! ’

elements.question: What two things does Jesus call us to do as we begin the Christian life?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus calls us to repent and to believe the gospel. Repentance means turning away from sin; belief means trusting in the good news of what Jesus has done.
elements.questionHint:
Look at the two commands Jesus gives at the end of the verse.
Can you name them both?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup>Therefore, just as you received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to live your lives in him, <sup>7</sup>rooted and built up in him and established in the faith just as you were taught, and overflowing with thankfulness.

elements.question: How do we continue in the Christian life?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: We continue in the Christian life the same way we began it — by receiving Christ as Lord and living in him. Paul describes this as being rooted and built up in Christ, established in the faith as we were taught, and overflowing with thankfulness.
elements.questionHint:
Paul says we should continue ’just as’ we began.
What does that tell you about how the start and the middle of the Christian life relate to each other?

elements.text:
The Christian life is a life of repentance and faith. That’s how it starts, and that’s how it should continue. Christians are fairly good at continuing with faith because we don’t think faith is something we should leave behind. But we can be embarrassed about repentance. We can think that repentance is great at the start of the Christian life, but that it is something to grow out of.
Mature Christians can be embarrassed to admit that they need to repent of anything. It’s OK to admit sin generally (‘We are all sinners in need of grace’) but not specifically (‘I still struggle with bad temper, or lust...’).

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup>If we say we do not bear the guilt of sin, we are deceiving ourselves and the truth is not in us. <sup>9</sup>But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous, forgiving us our sins and cleansing us from all unrighteousness.

elements.question: Why is it a problem to pretend we don’t have struggles with sin?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John says that if we claim to have no sin, we are deceiving ourselves and the truth is not in us. Pretending we have no struggles with sin is a form of self-deception — it cuts us off from the forgiveness and cleansing that God offers to those who honestly confess.
elements.questionHint: According to verse 8, what happens inside us when we deny our sinfulness — and what do we miss out on by not confessing (verse 9)?

elements.text: Pretending there are no problems, when of course there are, breeds hypocrisy. Pretending leads to ignoring problems - which stalls spiritual growth, and sets you up for a fall. Sin loves darkness. When you keep it in the dark, it grows. It shouldn’t be like that. Repentance and faith start the Christian life, and they continue the Christian life. When we repent, we turn to Jesus and we turn from sin - the two things go together. They go together at the start of the Christian race, as well as in the middle, and all the way to the end of the Christian race. So, as you do these studies, be serious about faith in Jesus, and be serious about repentance from sin.

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup>Now this is the gospel message we have heard from him and announce to you: God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all. <sup>6</sup>If we say we have fellowship with him and yet keep on walking in the darkness, we are lying and not practicing the truth. <sup>7</sup>But if we walk in the light as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship with one another and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.

elements.question: Why is it important to fight against sin?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Because God is light and there is no darkness in him at all. If we keep walking in sin (darkness) while claiming fellowship with God, we are living a lie. Fighting sin matters because it is the path to genuine fellowship with God and with one another, and it is how we experience the ongoing cleansing of Jesus’ blood.
elements.questionHint:
What does John say happens to our relationship with God if we keep walking in darkness?
What becomes possible when we walk in the light?

elements.text: What does your ’Growth Graph’ look like?

If you are not growing, it’s worth asking: ‘Am I really a Christian? Have I turned from sin and turned to Christ?’. If you haven’t put your faith in Christ, that would explain why you aren’t growing in Him. But, if you have turned from sin to Christ, and yet are not growing in Him, it’s still worth asking some hard questions. If you are not growing, something is wrong.
There are five graphs. The first graph shows a beautifully smooth growth-path. Your physical height would grow like this, but Christian growth isn’t the same. There are successes and there are setbacks. There are ups and there are downs. Real life is never so uniform.

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup>For we all stumble in many ways. If someone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect individual, able to control the entire body as well.

elements.question: Should we expect the Christian life to be free of ’stumbles’? (Why?)
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: No. James says plainly that ’we all stumble in many ways.’ Only a perfect person — someone who never stumbles in speech — would have complete mastery over the whole body. Since no one is perfect, stumbles are a normal part of the Christian life, not a sign that faith has failed.
elements.questionHint:
James uses the word ’all’.
What does that tell you about who is expected to stumble, and how often?

elements.text: Even Graph 2 is unrealistically predictable. Its ups and downs are modest and neat. The ’setbacks’ are almost elegant. Real life is more disappointing and less predictable.

elements.passageText: <sup>21</sup>So I find this law at work: When I want to do good, evil is present with me. <sup>22</sup>For I delight in the law of God in my inner being. <sup>23</sup>But I see a different law at work in my body—a law that fights against the law of my mind and imprisons me under the law of sin that is at work in my body.

elements.question: Why is it hard to grow in Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul describes an inner conflict: even when he wants to do good, evil is present within him. There is a ’law of sin’ at work in his body that fights against his desire to obey God and, in a sense, takes him prisoner. Growing in Christ is hard because this internal battle is real and ongoing — even for mature believers like Paul.
elements.questionHint:
Paul describes two opposing forces at work inside him.
What are they?
How does that conflict explain why growth is a struggle?

elements.text: Graph 3 is closer to what might be a more ’normal’ experience of Christian growth. There is growth, over time, but it is not smooth. There are advances and there are setbacks. On a short timescale, you can’t always tell whether things are improving or not. But over a longer timescale, you can see what the Holy Spirit has been doing in someone’s life. This is normal and good.

elements.alt: Graph 3: A growth chart showing uneven but generally upward spiritual progress over time
elements.caption: Graph 3

elements.text: But sometimes we end up with something more like Graph 4. For this person, there was spiritual growth for a while, but then something went wrong. Maybe they can identify the moment when it started to go wrong, or maybe they can’t. But, looking back, it’s obvious something has happened. Their growth has stalled.

elements.alt: Graph 4: A growth chart showing initial spiritual progress that levels off and stalls
elements.caption: Graph 4

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>’To the angel of the church in Sardis write: This is the message of the one who holds the seven spirits of God and the seven stars: I know your deeds, that you have a reputation that you are alive, but you are dead. <sup>2</sup>Wake up then, and strengthen what remains that was about to die, for I have not found your deeds complete in the sight of my God. <sup>3</sup>Therefore, remember what you received and heard, and obey it, and repent. If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will never know at what hour I will come against you.

elements.question: Is it OK to settle for getting ’stuck’ in the Christian life? (Why?)
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: No. Jesus’ words to the church in Sardis show how serious it is to become spiritually stuck. He describes them as having a reputation for being alive but actually being dead — and warns that if they do not wake up, repent, and return to what they first received, there will be real consequences. Settling for stagnation is not a neutral option.
elements.questionHint:
What does Jesus say he will do if this church does not wake up?
Does that sound like something they should be comfortable with?

elements.text: Maybe you can identify with Graph 3. If so, these studies will encourage you to keep going. But maybe you are closer to Graph 4 (or to something worse)! My prayer is that, as you read on, God will use these notes to give you a chance to change course. God wants all His children to grow in Jesus. He wants you to grow in Jesus. If you have stalled in your growth, it doesn’t have to stay that way. Your growth can be restarted. And, if you fix your eyes again on Jesus Christ, it will be. Graph 4 can turn into Graph 5.

elements.alt: Graph 5: A growth chart showing stalled spiritual progress that resumes and climbs again
elements.caption: Graph 5

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup>And some of you were these things. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.

elements.question: How does the Bible encourage us, that we can grow in Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul reminds the Corinthians that, whatever they used to be, they have been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of Jesus and by the Spirit of God. This is enormously encouraging: no past sin or pattern of failure defines us. Because of what Christ has already done, genuine change is possible — we are not stuck with who we were.
elements.questionHint:
Paul says ’some of you were these things’.
What tense is that?
What does it imply about the possibility of real change?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup>For I am confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will perfect it until the day of Christ Jesus.

elements.question: How else?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul is confident that God himself, who started the good work in us, will carry it through to completion. Our growth does not depend solely on our own effort or willpower — God is committed to finishing what he began in every believer, right up to the day of Christ Jesus.
elements.questionHint: Who does Paul say started the good work in believers — and if God started it, what does that tell you about whether he will see it through?

elements.text:
Listen to Paul’s story:

I was at school when I first put my faith in Jesus Christ. I was glad to be accepted and forgiven by Jesus. Life stopped being about obeying rules. The gospel was such good news that I wanted to make it known to others. I loved following Jesus. But then things started to cool down. After school I wanted a lucrative job. There were sins I struggled with. My growth as a Christian slowed down. I didn’t know what had gone wrong, or how to put it right.
Paul’s story is a common ’Graph 4’ pattern. Jesus does not want that to be your experience, and it doesn’t need to be.

elements.text: Growth — and Obedience to Jesus

Suppose your friend falls into a septic tank. He calls out, ‘Help! Help! Save me!’ so you pull him out. He says, ‘Thank you very much,‘ recovers his breath, and jumps back in. Then the whole thing repeats: he calls for help, you pull him out, he recovers and then jumps back in again. How many times are you going to pull him out?

How many times can you pull him out before you decide he isn’t serious about being ’saved’ from the tank? If he wants to be in the tank, he can’t be saved from the tank. It’s like that with us, Jesus and sin. Jesus calls us to come to Him to be saved from sin, guilt, shame, wrath, and judgement. But, until we do want to be saved from what holds us captive, Jesus does not save us. That’s why salvation and discipleship must go together.

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup>Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, <sup>20</sup>teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you. And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age.’

elements.question: The Great Commission* is not about ’conversion’. (1) What is it about? (2) What exactly are Jesus’ disciples commanded to obey?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: (1) The Great Commission is about making disciples — people who are baptised and taught to obey. It is about ongoing formation, not just a moment of decision. (2) Jesus says his disciples are to be taught to obey everything he has commanded — the full scope of his teaching, not a selected portion.
elements.questionHint:
What is the main verb Jesus gives in verse 19?
Is it ’convert’, or something else?
What does the teaching in verse 20 involve?

elements.question: Matthew 28:19-20 is often referred to as ’The Great Commission’.

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup>My commandment is this: Love one another just as I have loved you. <sup>13</sup>No one has greater love than this—that one lays down his life for his friends. <sup>14</sup>You are my friends if you do what I command you. <sup>15</sup>I no longer call you slaves, because the slave does not understand what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because I have revealed to you everything I heard from my Father.

elements.question: Just before his crucifixion, Jesus explains what it means to love him and to be his friends. Friendship with Jesus is unique. Why?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus’ friendship is unique for at least two reasons. First, it is a friendship that cost him everything — he defines the greatest love as laying down one’s life for one’s friends, which is exactly what he is about to do. Second, unlike a master who keeps servants in the dark, Jesus shares with his friends everything he has heard from the Father. It is a friendship of radical sacrifice and radical transparency.
elements.questionHint: In what two ways does Jesus describe what makes his friendship different from a typical master-servant relationship?

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup>But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the honor both now and on that eternal day.

elements.question: Growing in obedience is not the only aspect of growing in Jesus. What does Peter say we are to grow in? (He mentions two things.)
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter says we are to grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. Growing in grace means deepening our understanding and experience of God’s undeserved love and acceptance. Growing in knowledge means coming to know Christ more fully — who he is, what he has done, and what he calls us to.
elements.questionHint:
Peter uses two nouns joined by ’and’.
Can you spot both of them?
What do you think each one involves?

elements.text: Growing in grace includes growing in understanding that you are accepted by God. His love doesn’t depend on your performance. Obedience has a place, but it is not the foundation. God won’t stop loving you. He loves you not because of what you do, but because of what Jesus has already done.

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup>For while we were still helpless, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. <sup>7</sup>(For rarely will anyone die for a righteous person, though for a good person perhaps someone might possibly dare to die.) <sup>8</sup>But God demonstrates his own love for us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

elements.question: What had we done / what were we like, when Christ died for us?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: We were helpless, ungodly, and sinners. We had done nothing to deserve Christ’s death — in fact, we were in no position to help ourselves at all. Paul’s point is that God’s love was not triggered by anything good in us; Christ died for us precisely when we were at our worst.
elements.questionHint:
Paul uses three different words to describe our condition when Christ died.
Can you find all three?
What do they have in common?

elements.text: That timing is important. Christ didn’t save us because we learned to obey Him! He has already come to save us, and because of that we learn to obey Him. We love, because He first loved us. We serve, because He first served.

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup>For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, how much more, since we have been reconciled, will we be saved by his life?

elements.question: Why can we be confident that our salvation is already secure?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul argues from the greater to the lesser: if God reconciled us to himself when we were his enemies — which was the hardest thing — how much more certain is it that he will keep saving us now that we are his friends? Our salvation is secure because it rests on what Christ has already accomplished, not on our ongoing worthiness.
elements.questionHint: Paul uses a ’how much more’ argument — if God did the harder thing when we were enemies, what does that logically guarantee now that we are reconciled?

elements.passageText: It trains us 12to reject godless ways and worldly desires and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age,

elements.question: What is the connection between grace and godliness?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Grace is not merely the starting point of the Christian life — it actually trains us. The grace of God teaches us to say no to ungodliness and worldly desires, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives. Far from making us careless about holiness, grace is the engine that produces godliness.
elements.questionHint:
The passage says grace ’trains us’.
What exactly does it train us to do?
What does that suggest about the relationship between receiving grace and living a godly life?

elements.text: Growth — and Knowledge of Christ
Spiritual growth involves more than just knowledge, but it doesn’t involve less. You cannot know someone if you don’t know about them.

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup>More than that, I now regard all things as liabilities compared to the far greater value of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord, for whom I have suffered the loss of all things—indeed, I regard them as dung!—that I may gain Christ, <sup>9</sup>and be found in him, not because I have my own righteousness derived from the law, but because I have the righteousness that comes by way of Christ’s faithfulness—a righteousness from God that is in fact based on Christ’s faithfulness. <sup>10</sup>My aim is to know him, to experience the power of his resurrection, to share in his sufferings, and to be like him in his death, <sup>11</sup>and so, somehow, to attain to the resurrection from the dead.

elements.question: Why does Paul himself want to grow in knowing Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul wants to know Christ because knowing him surpasses the value of everything else combined — he counts all his former achievements and privileges as worthless by comparison. More specifically, he wants to be found in Christ with Christ’s righteousness (not his own), to experience resurrection power, to share in Christ’s sufferings, and ultimately to attain the resurrection from the dead. Knowing Christ is the whole goal.
elements.questionHint:
Paul lists several specific things he hopes to gain or experience through knowing Christ in verses 9–11.
Can you identify them?

elements.passageText: this is 13until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God—a mature person, attaining to the measure of Christ’s full stature.

elements.question: Why does Paul want others to grow in knowing Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul wants others to grow in the knowledge of the Son of God because that knowledge leads to maturity — specifically, to reaching the full measure of Christ’s stature. This is not just a personal goal but a communal one: the whole church is to attain unity in faith and knowledge together, growing up into Christ-like completeness.
elements.questionHint:
What does Paul say is the end result of growing together in knowledge of the Son of God?
Is this goal for individuals only, or for the whole church?

elements.text: If we are serious about knowing Jesus, we need to know about Him. We learn that through His Word. We also need to know Him. We need to follow Him, trust His lordship, and depend on Him. We grow as we put our knowledge about Christ into practice, and as we trust Him because we know Him.

elements.text: Growth — and Ageing and Maturity

Growth is about more than just allowing time to pass. Ageing is automatic; growing is not, and maturing is not. You can get older without growing in maturity or wisdom or godliness. Some of us get stuck as baby Christians. That is not what Jesus wants for us, and it is not what God intends for us.

elements.passageText: <sup>28</sup>We proclaim him by instructing and teaching all people with all wisdom so that we may present every person mature in Christ.

elements.question: What does Paul see as the end goal of all his teaching and preaching?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul’s ultimate goal in all his teaching and preaching is to present every person mature in Christ. It is not simply to get people to believe, or to grow the church numerically — it is to see each individual become fully mature in their relationship with Christ.
elements.questionHint: What does Paul say he is working towards at the end of the verse — and notice it says ’every person’, not just some?

elements.text: We will not be fully mature in Christ until we reach the New Creation. But already, here and now, we are to be growing in maturity. This is not easy, but it is not hopeless either. There can be discouragements and obstacles along the way. But we are more likely to overcome those obstacles if we are following the right path towards maturity.

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup>Therefore, just as you received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to live your lives in him, <sup>7</sup>rooted and built up in him and established in the faith just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.

elements.question: What is the route to maturity in Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The route to maturity is to continue living in Christ in the same way we first received him — as Lord. This involves being rooted and built up in him, established in the faith as we were taught, and living with an attitude of overflowing thankfulness. Maturity comes not by moving beyond Christ, but by going deeper into him.
elements.questionHint:
Paul uses four phrases to describe what ’continuing in Christ’ looks like.
Can you identify them?
What do they have in common?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup>’Listen! A sower went out to sow. <sup>4</sup>And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it. <sup>5</sup>Other seed fell on rocky ground where it did not have much soil, and it sprang up at once because the soil was not deep. <sup>6</sup>When the sun came up it was scorched, and because it did not have sufficient root, it withered. <sup>7</sup>Other seed fell among the thorns, and they grew up and choked it, and it did not produce grain. <sup>8</sup>But other seed fell on good soil and produced grain, sprouting and growing; some yielded thirty times as much, some sixty, and some a hundred times.’ <sup>9</sup>And he said, ‘Whoever has ears to hear had better listen!’

elements.question: Why is it important to have our spiritual ’roots’ in the right place?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Without deep roots, growth cannot last. The seed on rocky ground springs up quickly but withers under pressure because it has no depth. Seed among thorns is choked and never matures. Only seed in good soil — with proper roots — produces lasting fruit. Spiritually, if we are not deeply rooted in Christ, difficulties and distractions will prevent us from ever reaching maturity.
elements.questionHint:
What happens to the seed that sprouts quickly but has no deep root?
What caused it to wither?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>How blessed is the one who does not follow the advice of the wicked, or stand in the pathway with sinners, or sit in the assembly of scoffers! <sup>2</sup>Instead he finds pleasure in obeying the Lord’s commands; he meditates on his commands day and night. <sup>3</sup>He is like a tree planted by flowing streams; it yields its fruit at the proper time, and its leaves never wither. Success attends whatever he does. <sup>4</sup>Not so with the wicked! Instead they are like wind-driven chaff. <sup>5</sup>For this reason the wicked cannot withstand judgment, nor can sinners join the assembly of the godly. <sup>6</sup>Certainly the Lord guards the way of the godly, but the way of the wicked ends in destruction.

elements.question: Why else is it important to have our spiritual ’roots’ in the right place?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Psalm 1 shows that where our roots go determines our fruitfulness and our final destiny. The person rooted in God’s word is like a tree by a stream — always fruitful, never withering, with God guarding their way. But the rootless (the wicked) are like chaff — they cannot stand when it matters most and their way ends in destruction. Right roots mean life; wrong roots mean ruin.
elements.questionHint:
Compare the two images in the Psalm — a tree by a stream versus wind-driven chaff.
What does each image say about the outcome of where a person has planted their roots?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup>But I have this against you: You have departed from your first love! <sup>5</sup>Therefore, remember from what high state you have fallen and repent! Do the deeds you did at the first; if not, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place—that is, if you do not repent.

elements.question: Why is it dangerous to move away from our foundation in Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The church in Ephesus had drifted from their first love — and Jesus treats this very seriously. He warns that if they do not remember, repent, and return to their earlier devotion, he will remove their lampstand. Moving away from our foundation in Christ is not a minor adjustment; it puts our very existence as a light-bearing community in jeopardy.
elements.questionHint:
What does Jesus threaten to do to this church if they do not repent?
How serious does that sound to you?

elements.passageText: <sup>20</sup>But our citizenship is in heaven—and we also eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ, <sup>21</sup>who will transform these humble bodies of ours into the likeness of his glorious body by means of that power by which he is able to subject all things to himself.

elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage

elements.text: This is an amazing destiny — being raised to new life, in a new body just like Jesus was, and being conformed to the image of God’s own Son! It is not about gaining Bible knowledge or ticking years off the calendar. It is about our character becoming more like Jesus’ character. We take on more of a family resemblance as we grow into our identity as God’s children in Christ.

Begin a Personal ’Gospel-Growth Plan’

Don’t choose something general:
❌ ’Growing as a Christian’ is admirable in principle, but vague in practice.

elements.text:
John Owen’s quote (above) is short and sharp, but very true. If we nurture sins — even little sins — we give them time to grow into killers. This chapter is titled ’Sin holds us back’, but Owen might say that’s too weak. Sin doesn’t just hold us back; it destroys us, it kills us, it ruins us. God agrees. In Genesis 4:7 God pictures sin as a predator — like a lion crouching at our door, ready to spring, pounce, and devour. Will we let it? Will we ’master’ this predator — or will we become prey?

Thomas learned the danger of sin the hard way. He grew up in church, heavily involved in the choir, and was well respected. Others his age looked up to him as a model Christian. But he had a secret. He had fallen into sexual immorality and abortion. Repeatedly. He felt like a fraud, like his Christian life was over, like his faith was destroyed. Sin had pounced on him, like a predator, and he did not see any way back.

We will look carefully at this predator, so that we are ready to escape it, master it, and kill it — so that it is not killing us.

elements.text: The First Sin

Sin loves deception. The serpent appears unannounced in Genesis 3, and he quickly demonstrates that he is a master of deception. But he doesn’t use outright, 100% falsehood. He is more subtle than that.

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>Now the serpent was more shrewd than any of the wild animals the Lord God had made. He said to the woman, ‘Is it really true that God said, "You must not eat from any tree of the orchard"?’ <sup>2</sup>The woman said to the serpent, ‘We may eat of the fruit from the trees of the orchard; <sup>3</sup>but concerning the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of the orchard God said, "You must not eat from it, and you must not touch it, or else you will die."’ <sup>4</sup>The serpent said to the woman, ‘Surely you will not die, <sup>5</sup>for God knows that when you eat from it your eyes will open and you will be like divine beings who know good and evil.’ <sup>6</sup>When the woman saw that the tree produced fruit that was good for food, was attractive to the eye, and was desirable for making one wise, she took some of its fruit and ate it. She also gave some of it to her husband who was with her, and he ate it. <sup>7</sup>Then the eyes of both of them opened, and they knew they were naked; so they sewed fig leaves together and made coverings for themselves. <sup>8</sup>Then the man and his wife heard the sound of the Lord God moving about in the orchard at the breezy time of the day, and they hid from the Lord God among the trees of the orchard.

elements.question: What tactics does the serpent use to mislead and deceive?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The serpent uses several tactics: he begins by misquoting God to sow doubt (‘Did God really say you must not eat from any tree?’), then flatly contradicts God’s warning about death (‘Surely you will not die’). He also plants a slander against God’s motives — implying that God is withholding something good from them. Finally, he appeals to Eve’s desires: the fruit looks good, it is attractive, and it promises wisdom. The deception works by mixing just enough truth with falsehood to make it plausible.
elements.questionHint:
Look at what the serpent says in verses 1, 4, and 5.
In each case, is he distorting, denying, or slandering?
What is he trying to make Eve doubt?

elements.question: What mistakes does Eve make in how she responds to the serpent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Eve makes several mistakes. First, she engages with the serpent’s distortion rather than rejecting it outright. Second, she slightly misquotes God’s command herself — adding ’you must not touch it’, which God had not said. Third, she allows herself to be swayed by the fruit’s physical appeal (good for food, attractive, desirable for wisdom) rather than holding firmly to God’s word. Fourth, Adam, who was with her, says nothing and also eats — and she shares the fruit without any resistance. Together they prioritise their own judgement over God’s clear instruction.
elements.questionHint:
Compare what God actually said in chapter 2 with what Eve says in verse 3.
Do you notice any difference?
In verse 6, what three things draw her towards the fruit?

elements.text:
Superficially, the serpent’s claims turn out to be ’true’. By the end of the chapter Adam and Eve: (i) are still alive (not ’surely dead’), (ii) the ’eyes of both of them were opened’ (they become ashamed of their nakedness), and (iii) God declares, ‘The man has now become like one of us, knowing good and evil’. But the thrust of the serpent’s temptation implied that, if they seized control of their destiny, things would become much better. It does not turn out that way. Things become so much worse: they move from being at home in the garden to exile; from fellowship with God to exclusion; from honour to shame; from innocence to guilt; from security to fear; from blessing to curse; and from the sphere of life to the sphere of death.

Many of the ’best’ lies are half-truths (or partial-truths or distorted-truths). It is hard to poison someone by getting them to eat 100% pure poison. It is much easier to give them tasty food with a percentage of poison mixed in. Deception is the same. It is easier to get someone to believe a lie if you mix it with some truth. That gives the lie a ring of truth it would otherwise lack. That’s the serpent’s strategy here, and, tragically, it works. Our world goes from being under blessing, to being under God’s curse. The curses of Genesis 3:14-19 do not undo the blessings of creation, they are layered on top of them. But God has not given up on His purposes of blessing.

elements.passageText: <sup>21</sup>The Lord God made garments from skin for Adam and his wife, and clothed them.

elements.question: God banishes Adam and Eve from the Garden, but before he banishes them, there are some hints of hope. What are they?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Even in the midst of judgement, God acts with care: he makes proper garments of skin for Adam and Eve and clothes them. This is a hint that God has not abandoned them — he is still providing for them and covering their shame. The fact that an animal apparently died to provide these skins also hints, very early in the Bible, at the idea that a substitute’s death can cover human sin and shame.
elements.questionHint:
What does God personally do for Adam and Eve before sending them out?
What might the fact that it required animal skin suggest about how their shame is being covered?

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup>And I will put hostility between you and the woman and between your offspring and her offspring; her offspring will attack your head, and you will attack her offspring’s heel.’

elements.question: What else hints at hope after the fall?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God promises that there will be ongoing hostility between the serpent and the woman’s offspring, but crucially, that the woman’s offspring will strike the serpent’s head — a fatal blow — even while the serpent strikes his heel. This is the first hint in the Bible of a coming deliverer who will ultimately defeat the one who caused the fall, though at cost to himself. Christians read this as a foreshadowing of Christ’s victory over Satan through the cross.
elements.questionHint: In the conflict between the serpent and the woman’s offspring, which blow is fatal — the strike to the head or the strike to the heel — and what might that difference suggest?

elements.text: Sin Spreads

Sin doesn’t sit still. It spreads from Adam and Eve to their children, and from the eating of the fruit (which is seemingly minor, but profoundly rebellious) to other sins, all within a single generation.

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup>Abel also brought some of the firstborn of his flock—even the fattest of them. And the Lord was pleased with Abel and his offering, <sup>5</sup>but with Cain and his offering he was not pleased. So Cain became very angry, and his expression fell. <sup>6</sup>Then the Lord said to Cain, ‘Why are you angry, and why has your expression fallen? <sup>7</sup>If you do what is right, will you not be accepted? But if you do not do what is right, sin is crouching at the door. It desires to dominate you, but you must subdue it.’ <sup>8</sup>Cain said to his brother Abel, ‘Let’s go out to the field.’ While they were in the field, Cain attacked his brother Abel and killed him.

elements.question: Adam eats the fruit and is ashamed; but it doesn’t end there. How does sin spread?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Sin spreads to the next generation immediately. Cain’s jealousy over God’s acceptance of Abel’s offering turns to anger, and despite God’s direct warning that sin is crouching at the door and must be subdued, Cain does not resist it. The sin of Adam’s family has escalated from eating forbidden fruit to the first murder — all within a single generation. Sin passes from parents to children and grows in intensity.
elements.questionHint:
God warns Cain that sin is ’crouching at the door’ and wants to dominate him.
What does Cain choose to do with that warning?
What is the result?

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup>Lamech said to his wives: ‘Adah and Zillah! Listen to me! You wives of Lamech, hear what I say! I have killed a man for wounding me, a young man for hurting me. <sup>24</sup>If Cain is to be avenged seven times as much, then Lamech seventy-seven times!’

elements.question: How else does sin spread?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Sin not only spreads to the next generation — it escalates in intensity and becomes boastful. Lamech, just a few generations after Cain, kills a man merely for wounding him and then openly boasts about it to his wives. Where Cain’s sin was terrible, Lamech’s vengeance is out of all proportion and he glories in it. Sin grows more extreme and more shameless over time when left unchecked.
elements.questionHint:
Compare Cain’s killing of Abel with Lamech’s attitude in these verses.
What has changed, not just in the act, but in the attitude towards the sin?

elements.text: Even a ’little’ sin (like eating the fruit) is far from harmless, because it spreads and grows. Suppose you are a farmer, and someone sows a few ’tiny’ seeds in your farm, but they are seeds of a vigorous weed. They are tiny, but they grow into something that causes great harm. Sin is like that — an evil seed that grows and spreads and poisons and corrupts. Sometimes we think we can play with sin and get away with it. We think we can touch the darkness and then let go. But it swallows us whole.

elements.text: Sin as Refusal
The Bible has many ways of describing sin, including as types of refusal.

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup>For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of people who suppress the truth by their unrighteousness, <sup>19</sup>because what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain to them. <sup>20</sup>For since the creation of the world his invisible attributes—his eternal power and divine nature—have been clearly seen, because they are understood through what has been made. So people are without excuse. <sup>21</sup>For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give him thanks, but they became futile in their thoughts and their senseless hearts were darkened. <sup>22</sup>Although they claimed to be wise, they became fools <sup>23</sup>and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for an image resembling mortal human beings or birds or four-footed animals or reptiles.

elements.question: What do we learn about how sin can lead to a refusal of knowledge?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says that knowledge of God is clearly available to everyone through creation — his eternal power and divine nature are plain for all to see. Yet people actively suppress this truth. Rather than receiving the knowledge God has made available, sin drives people to refuse it — their thinking becomes futile, their hearts darkened, and they end up trading the glory of the immortal God for idols. Sin doesn’t just make people ignorant; it makes them actively resistant to what they already, at some level, know.
elements.questionHint: Paul says God has made knowledge of himself ’plain’ — so why, according to verses 21-23, do people end up in darkness despite that?

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup>For if the message spoken through angels had credibility, and every transgression and act of disobedience received a just reward, <sup>3</sup>how will we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? It was first communicated through the Lord and was confirmed to us by those who heard him,

elements.question: And how else can sin lead to a refusal of knowledge?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Here the refusal of knowledge takes the form of neglect. The author warns that if even the old message given through angels carried serious consequences for those who disobeyed, how much more serious is it to ignore the great salvation announced by the Lord himself? Sin can lead us to drift past saving knowledge not through dramatic rejection, but through simple carelessness — paying it no attention.
elements.questionHint:
The writer doesn’t say people ’rejected’ salvation but that they ’neglected’ it.
What is the difference?
Why might neglect still be a form of refusing knowledge?

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup>Little children, let no one deceive you: The one who practices righteousness is righteous, just as Jesus is righteous.

elements.question: And how else?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John warns against being deceived about the connection between character and conduct. Sin can involve a refusal to accept what we actually know — namely, that a genuinely righteous person is known by actually practising righteousness. We can deceive ourselves into thinking we know God while our behaviour tells a different story. This is a refusal of knowledge about what true righteousness looks like.
elements.questionHint:
John says ’let no one deceive you’.
What specific piece of knowledge is someone at risk of being deceived about in this verse?

elements.passageText: <sup>14</sup>Yet death reigned from Adam until Moses even over those who did not sin in the same way as Adam (who is a type of the coming one).

elements.question: In what way(s) is God’s authority refused in this verse?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul makes the point that death — the consequence of Adam’s refusal to obey God — reigned even over people who had no specific commandment to break in the way Adam did. Adam’s sin was a direct defiance of a known command; but even where no such explicit law existed, the pattern of sin as a refusal of God’s right to rule had already been set. The universal reign of death is evidence that humanity as a whole has been living in refusal of God’s authority since the beginning.
elements.questionHint: If death reigned even over those who hadn’t broken a specific command like Adam, what does that tell you about how deeply Adam’s original act of refusal has affected everyone?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup>He said to me, ‘Son of man, I am sending you to the house of Israel, to rebellious nations who have rebelled against me; both they and their fathers have revolted against me to this very day. <sup>4</sup>The people to whom I am sending you are obstinate and hard-hearted, and you must say to them, "This is what the Sovereign Lord says." <sup>5</sup>As for them, whether they listen or not—for they are a rebellious house—they will know that a prophet has been among them.

elements.question: And in what way(s) is God’s authority refused in this verse?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God describes Israel as rebellious, obstinate, and hard-hearted — and notes that this rebellion has continued across generations (‘they and their fathers’). Their refusal is not passive indifference but active, persistent revolt against the Sovereign Lord. Even the possibility that they won’t listen is anticipated and accepted by God, who sends Ezekiel anyway. Sin here is a deliberate, multigenerational refusal to submit to God’s word and authority.
elements.questionHint: God uses several strong words to describe Israel’s attitude — ‘rebellious’, ‘obstinate’, ‘hard-hearted’ — what pattern do those words together describe about how they have treated God’s authority?

elements.passageText: For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give him thanks, 21but they became futile in their thoughts and their senseless hearts were darkened.

elements.question: Sin can also involve being ungrateful. What is refused in this verse?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: What is refused here is twofold: the glorifying of God as God, and thankfulness to him. Even people who knew God chose not to honour him as God or to give thanks. Ingratitude is not merely a social failing — Paul frames it as a form of sin, a refusal to acknowledge God’s goodness and give him the credit he is due. The consequences are serious: futile thinking and a darkened heart.
elements.questionHint:
Paul says they ’knew God’ but still refused two specific things.
Can you name both of them?
What do they have in common?

elements.passageText: <sup>40</sup>But if they confess their iniquity and the iniquity of their ancestors—their unfaithfulness by which they were unfaithful to me and also how they walked in opposition to me—

elements.question: How did the Israelites refuse to be in relationship with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The verse speaks of their unfaithfulness — they were unfaithful to God and walked in opposition to him. Relationship with God requires faithfulness and loyalty, but they refused both. Walking ’in opposition’ to God is a vivid image of actively moving against him rather than with him. The fact that this pattern needed to be confessed generation by generation shows how deeply embedded the refusal of relationship had become.
elements.questionHint: The passage uses two phrases to describe what Israel did — ‘unfaithful’ and ’walked in opposition’ — what kind of relationship does each phrase picture, and what does refusing both look like?

elements.passageText: <sup>25</sup>They exchanged the truth of God for a lie and worshiped and served the creation rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever! Amen.

elements.question: Ultimately, sin is a refusal of God himself. How do we see that?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul describes the ultimate form of sin as an exchange: swapping the truth of God for a lie, and transferring worship and service away from the Creator to created things. This is not just breaking rules — it is the wholesale replacement of God himself with something else. The creature refuses the Creator: they don’t merely disobey God, they redirect the devotion that is his due to things he has made. That is the deepest form of refusal.
elements.questionHint:
Paul uses the word ’exchanged’.
What exactly was exchanged for what?
What does that tell you about where their ultimate loyalty ended up?

elements.passageText: <sup>30</sup>Love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength.’

elements.question: What is the opposite of refusing God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The opposite of refusing God is loving him with everything we have — heart, soul, mind, and strength. Where sin withholds, the greatest commandment demands total, wholehearted devotion. The fourfold repetition of ’all’ makes clear that this is not partial loyalty or occasional attention, but a complete and unreserved orientation of our entire selves towards God.
elements.questionHint:
Jesus says ’all’ four times in this verse.
What does that repeated emphasis tell you about what total acceptance of God (the opposite of refusal) actually looks like?

elements.text: We refuse God, or we love Him with everything we’ve got. Sin is refusing the good that God wants for us, and trying to grasp our own ’good’ instead. There are many opportunities for refusal: we can refuse knowledge of God, His authority, His goodness. We can even refuse God Himself.

elements.text: The Effects of Sin

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup>For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of people who suppress the truth by their unrighteousness,

elements.question: What effects does sin have on our relationship with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Sin draws the wrath of God. Paul says the wrath of God is currently being revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness — specifically against those who suppress the truth. Sin does not leave the relationship with God neutral; it places us under his just anger. The suppression of truth is not an innocent act — it is the active distortion of what God has made plain, and it has real consequences for how God relates to us.
elements.questionHint:
What specific response does Paul say God has towards ungodliness and unrighteousness?
Does that suggest the relationship between God and the sinner is comfortable or troubled?

elements.passageText: <sup>31</sup>because he has set a day on which he is going to judge the world in righteousness, by a man whom he designated, having provided proof to everyone by raising him from the dead.’

elements.question: And what else does sin do to our relationship with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Sin brings us into the category of those who will face God’s judgement. Paul declares that God has already fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness, through the risen Jesus. Every person living in sin stands under the certainty of that coming judgement. The resurrection of Jesus is the proof that this is real — it is not a distant threat but a confirmed appointment.
elements.questionHint:
Paul says God has ’set a day’.
What does the fact that this day is already fixed tell you about the certainty of judgement for those who continue in sin?

elements.passageText: <sup>21</sup>And you were at one time strangers and enemies in your minds as expressed through your evil deeds,

elements.question: And what else does sin do to our relationship with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Sin makes us strangers and enemies of God. Paul says this estrangement is not just external — it originates in the mind, and it expresses itself through evil deeds. Sin produces a fundamental alienation from God: we become not just distant from him but hostile to him. The two words Paul uses — ‘strangers’ and ’enemies’ — describe both the relational distance and the active opposition that sin creates.
elements.questionHint: Paul uses two words to describe our pre-reconciliation relationship with God — ‘strangers’ and ’enemies’ — what is the difference between them, and which is more serious?

elements.passageText: For we too were once foolish, disobedient, misled, enslaved to various passions and desires, spending our lives in evil and envy, hateful and hating one another—3but when the kindness of God our Savior and his love for mankind appeared,

elements.question: How does sin affect our relationship with other people, and creation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul paints a bleak picture: sin leads to lives characterised by evil and envy, and a state of being hateful and hating one another. Relationships with others are poisoned — instead of love and goodwill, there is mutual hostility. Sin does not just damage our relationship with God; it corrupts every human relationship, turning people who were made for community into sources of harm to one another.
elements.questionHint:
Paul ends his description with ’hateful and hating one another’.
What does that double description suggest about how sin affects both what we are and what we do to those around us?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup>Do not trust a friend; do not rely on a companion. Guard your words from the one who lies in your embrace.

elements.question: And how else does sin affect our relationship with other people?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Sin destroys trust — even between the closest of people. Micah describes a world so corrupted by sin that you cannot trust your closest friend, your companion, or even the person in your own home. This is a picture of social breakdown at the most intimate level: sin reaches into the places where trust should be strongest and corrodes them. Relationships that should be safe become dangerous.
elements.questionHint:
Micah moves from ’friend’ to ’companion’ to ’the one who lies in your embrace’.
What does this progression tell you about how far sin’s damage to trust reaches?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup>But evil people and charlatans will go from bad to worse, deceiving others and being deceived themselves.

elements.question: And how else does sin affect our relationship with other people?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Sin spreads through deception — people who are in sin deceive others and are themselves deceived. This is a self-reinforcing cycle: those who are evil and those who are charlatans do not stay the same, they go from bad to worse. Sin damages relationships with others by turning them into occasions for manipulation and deception, while also trapping the sinner deeper in their own self-deception.
elements.questionHint:
Paul says evil people are both ’deceiving others’ and ’being deceived themselves’.
What does it mean that sin damages both what you do to others and what happens to you?

elements.passageText: <sup>3:16</sup>For where there is envy and selfish ambition, there is disorder and every evil practice. <sup>4:1</sup>Where do the conflicts and where do the quarrels among you come from? Is it not from this, that your passions are at war within your members? <sup>2</sup>You desire and you do not have; you murder and envy and you cannot obtain; you quarrel and fight. You do not have because you do not ask.

elements.question: And how else does sin affect our relationship with other people?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: James traces conflict and quarrel directly back to internal sinful desires. Where there is envy and selfish ambition, disorder and every evil practice follow. The passions that war inside us spill outward into conflict with others — fighting, quarrelling, and even murder. Sin does not stay internal; it becomes the engine of relational breakdown and social disorder. The root is within; the fruit poisons those around us.
elements.questionHint:
James asks where quarrels ’come from’ and then answers his own question.
What does his answer reveal about the real source of conflict between people?

elements.passageText: <sup>22</sup>Do not rob the poor because he is poor, and do not crush the afflicted at the city gate,

elements.question: And how else does sin affect our relationship with other people?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Sin drives the powerful to exploit the powerless. The proverb warns against robbing the poor precisely because of their poverty, and crushing the afflicted at the very place (the city gate) where they should receive justice. Sin corrupts relationships across social lines — it turns those with power into oppressors of the vulnerable, reversing the justice and care that God intends.
elements.questionHint:
The verse says not to rob the poor ’because he is poor’.
What does that phrase suggest about the particularly sinful nature of exploiting someone’s vulnerability?

elements.passageText: 3For we too were once foolish, disobedient, misled, enslaved to various passions and desires, spending our lives in evil and envy, hateful and hating one another.—but when the kindness of God our Savior and his love for mankind appeared,

elements.question: What effects does sin have on our self?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul describes sin’s effects on the self as comprehensive: it makes us foolish (poor judgement), disobedient (rebellious will), and misled (distorted thinking). Most damagingly, it enslaves us — we become captive to various passions and desires, with no real freedom. Sin does not liberate the self; it imprisons it, reducing the person to a slave of their own cravings.
elements.questionHint:
Paul uses the word ’enslaved’ to describe one of sin’s effects on the self.
What does slavery imply about how much freedom or control the sinner actually has over their own life?

elements.question: And what else does sin do to our self?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Sin also deceives the self. Paul says that evil people go from bad to worse and are not just deceiving others but being deceived themselves. The sinner does not see their situation clearly — they are caught in a self-reinforcing delusion. Sin doesn’t just make us behave badly; it warps our perception so that we can no longer accurately assess our own condition, making the problem harder and harder to escape.
elements.questionHint:
Paul says that along with deceiving others, sinful people are ’being deceived themselves’.
Who or what is doing the deceiving?
What might that mean for the sinner’s ability to see themselves clearly?

elements.text:
Christians can create hierarchies of sin, which are based more on what is respectable within their culture than on the Bible’s values. External and blatant sins are bad, but ’invisible’ sins are overlooked. For example, sexual sin is ’bad,‘ but pride, greed, and jealousy are tolerated and/or excused. Jesus did not conform to respectable hierarchies of sin.

That’s why the Pharisees hated Him, but the ’sinners’ listened (Mark 2:15-17). Don’t line yourself up with the Pharisees in that argument! You won’t grow if you don’t repent of your sin. Repentance is how you master the predator crouching at your door, that desires to have you. Turn from sin, and turn to Christ — that is how to kill sin before it kills you.

Here are 7 pairs of statements. Each pair defines opposite ends of a scale describing your view of God’s attitude towards you. On each line, choose the point that best represents your idea of how God sees you. The closer the point is to the statement, the more you think it’s like that.

elements.text: The Bible often describes God as our Father. Sometimes we turn to our own (earthly) fathers to understand what this means. Some will have done a better job than others. But the Bible is the right place to look to understand what sort of Father God is. It shows us where we stand before Him, and how He sees us. A big factor in that, is the question of whether we have come home to God.
The Lost Son (Luke 15:11-32)
Read through the parable of the lost son, and then answer these questions.
Character 1: The Younger Son

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup>The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of the property that will belong to me.’ So he divided the estate between them.

elements.question: What is unusual, or even rude, about the younger son’s behaviour? And what is surprising about the father’s response?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: In the culture of the day, asking for your inheritance while your father is still alive was deeply insulting — it was effectively wishing your father were dead. The son wants the father’s wealth without the relationship. What is surprising is the father’s response: rather than rebuking the son or refusing, he divides the estate and gives it to him. The father does not coerce loyalty; he allows the son to go, even at great personal cost.
elements.questionHint:
In the culture of the time, an inheritance was only received after a parent’s death.
What does the son’s demand therefore imply about how he views his father and their relationship?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup>After a few days, the younger son gathered together all he had and traveled to a distant country, where he squandered his wealth with extravagant living.

elements.question: How does the son use his freedom?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: He leaves quickly, travels as far away as possible from his father, and wastes everything he has been given on extravagant, reckless living. The freedom he demanded is used entirely for self-indulgence, with no thought for his father, his family, or the future. He converts relationship and inheritance into immediate personal pleasure.
elements.questionHint:
Notice the son goes to ’a distant country’.
What does the physical distance from his father suggest about the kind of freedom he was really looking for?

elements.passageText: <sup>14</sup>When he had spent everything, a severe famine took place in that country, and he began to be in need. <sup>15</sup>So he went and worked for one of the citizens of that country, who sent him to his fields to feed pigs.

elements.question: He gets to do everything he wants, but how does it end up?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: He runs out of money, a famine hits, and he finds himself in desperate need. Rather than being his own master, he is now entirely dependent on a stranger who sends him to feed pigs — the most degrading work imaginable for a Jewish young man. The freedom he chased has brought him not to abundance but to poverty, servitude, and humiliation.
elements.questionHint: The son wanted to be free and in control of his own life — looking at where he ends up in verse 15, how much freedom and control does he actually have now?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup>He was wanting to eat the pods that the pigs were eating, but no one gave him anything.

elements.question: What is tragic about this, especially for a Jewish boy?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: He has reached the absolute lowest point. Pigs were considered unclean animals under Jewish law, and contact with them was something a Jewish person would have considered deeply defiling. Now he is not just feeding them but longing to eat what they eat — and even that is denied him. The boy who demanded his father’s wealth is now below the level of the pigs he tends. He has lost everything, including his dignity.
elements.questionHint:
Pigs were considered ritually unclean in Jewish culture.
What does the fact that a Jewish boy is not only tending them but wanting to eat their food tell you about how far he has fallen?

elements.text:
Perhaps you can identify with this young man. It’s been many people’s story. God made us, and loves us, but we take it all for granted. God gets in our way. So, in our different ways, we leave home. We turn our backs on the God who loves us. Some of us march out of God’s front door: ‘I’ll be my own boss. I’ll do what I want, when I want.’

Others leave quietly through the back door. If that’s you, then you probably still believe in God, and go to church. But when it comes to important things, you do what you want; not what God wants. You have not made a fuss about it, but you are still far away from God — doing your own thing without reference to Him. That is what sin is — doing your own thing, forgetting about God, ignoring His standards, and living in His world without paying Him any real attention.

elements.question: Overall, how do you feel in your relationship with God? Do you mostly feel ’at home’ with Him, or do you feel more distant?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Your thoughts...

elements.text: Sin doesn’t always make you feel dreadful, not straight away. Sin can be fun. We all know that, because we have all enjoyed it. But it is a hollow sort of fun. We need more and more to satisfy us, and it is still never enough. Long-term we end up destroying ourselves. We end up in the pig-house. It’s no surprise it turns out like that when we reject God’s standards. He made us, He knows how we should live. Sin means making myself the most important thing in the universe — and that always brings with it bitterness, envy, and hatred. We hurt ourselves and we hurt others.
Character 2: The Loving Father

elements.passageText: 19I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired men.’ 20So he got up and went to his father. But while he was still a long way off his father saw him and felt compassion for him, and ran and embraced his neck and kissed him.

elements.question: What sort of reception does the son expect to get from his father?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The son expects to be demoted. He rehearses a speech admitting he is no longer worthy to be called a son and asks only to be treated as a hired servant. He expects a business transaction at best — not restoration. He is coming home not because he expects love but because he is desperate and has nowhere else to go. His expectations of his father are low.
elements.questionHint:
What is the son planning to ask his father to make him?
What does that tell you about what kind of welcome he thinks he deserves?

elements.text: We only get to know people on the outside. We worry that if other people knew all that we have thought, said, and done, then they would wish they didn’t! And if we are worried about what other people might think, then we certainly don’t want God to know what we are really like. But this story tells us that even though God knows everything about us, He still loves us and wants us back. There has never been a day when God has not thought of us; looking for some sign that we will come home.

elements.passageText: ’I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired men.’ So he got up and went to his father. But while he was still a long way off20his father saw him and felt compassion for him, and ran and embraced his neck and kissed him.

elements.question: Do you think the father has given up on his son? Why / Why not?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: No. The detail that the father saw him ’while he was still a long way off’ implies he was watching and waiting — he had not given up hope. He does not wait for the son to arrive and make his case; he runs to him. A father who had given up would not be scanning the horizon. His immediate compassion and physical embrace show that his love has never wavered, despite everything his son did.
elements.questionHint:
How was the father able to see his son ’while he was still a long way off’?
What does that suggest about what the father had been doing during his son’s absence?

elements.question: Sum up the father’s response in this verse, when he realises his son has come home.
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The father’s response is immediate, physical, and overwhelming: he feels compassion, runs to his son, embraces him, and kisses him — all before the son has said a word. There is no hesitation, no lecture, no conditions. The return of his son produces an outpouring of love that completely overtakes any thought of reproach.
elements.questionHint:
The verse describes four actions the father takes in quick succession.
Can you list them?
What do they together tell you about the father’s emotional state?

elements.passageText: <sup>22</sup>But the father said to his slaves, ‘Hurry! Bring out the best robe and put it on him! Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet! <sup>23</sup>Bring the fattened calf and kill it! Let us eat and celebrate,

elements.question: And what is the father’s response in these verses?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The father immediately restores the son to full honour: the best robe (not a servant’s), a ring (a sign of family authority and belonging), sandals (servants went barefoot, not sons), and a feast with the fattened calf reserved for special occasions. The son asked to be a servant; the father reinstates him as a son. Everything about the response is lavish, urgent, and joyful — nothing is held back.
elements.questionHint:
The son asked to be treated like a hired servant.
Look at the robe, ring, and sandals the father gives him.
What status does each item represent?
How does it compare to what the son requested?

elements.passageText: <sup>24</sup>because this son of mine was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found!’ So they began to celebrate.

elements.question: And what is the father’s response in this verse?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The father explains his joy in the most profound terms: his son was dead and is alive again, was lost and is found. He does not describe his son’s return in terms of behavioural improvement or a debt repaid — he describes it as a resurrection, a recovery of something precious that was gone. This is not relief; it is overwhelming joy at a life restored. And so they celebrate.
elements.questionHint:
The father doesn’t say ’my son was bad but now he’s better’ — he says ’he was dead and is alive again.’
What does that stronger language tell you about how the father understood the son’s time away?

elements.text: God wants us back, and, to show His love for us, He sent us His Son to take our place. That’s God’s great declaration to the world — He loves us and wants us home. Jesus didn’t deserve to die. We do; for all the wrong that we have done and the hurt that we have caused. But He died in our place so that we could come home to God, freely forgiven. That’s God’s offer of love to each of us. A new life that starts with Jesus.

elements.text: ‘God loves each of us as if there were only one of us.’ — Augustine of Hippo
