elements.text: The parable of the prodigal son is a story with an aim.

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>Now all the tax collectors and sinners were coming near to listen to him. <sup>2</sup>But both the Pharisees and the experts in the law were complaining, saying, ‘This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.’

elements.question: Who was Jesus originally aiming this story at?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The immediate audience includes both groups — the tax collectors and sinners who were drawing near to listen, and the Pharisees and experts in the law who were grumbling about Jesus’ willingness to welcome them. The parable is aimed especially at the religious critics: people who could not understand why a holy man would associate with the wrong sort. The older son in the story is a direct mirror of their attitude.
elements.questionHint: Luke gives us two groups in these verses — one drawing near to Jesus and one pulling away — which group do you think is most challenged by the parable of the lost son, and why?

elements.text: Character 3: The Listening Audience
For religious people, this parable’s punch comes with the older son.

elements.passageText: 28But the older brother became angry and refused to go in. And his father came out and began to urge him.

elements.question: How does the older son respond when he hears of his brother’s return?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: He becomes angry and refuses to go in to the celebration. Rather than sharing his father’s joy at the return of a lost brother, he stands outside in protest. His response is the mirror image of the father’s: where the father ran towards the returning son, the older brother draws back and separates himself from the family reunion.
elements.questionHint: While the father ran towards his returning son, the older brother moves in the opposite direction — what does that contrast tell you about the difference between the father’s heart and the older son’s?

elements.passageText: But the older brother became angry and refused to go in. And his father came out28and began to urge him.

elements.question: How does his father respond to this response from the older son?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The father comes out — leaving the celebration — and urges the older son to come in. Just as the father ran to the younger son who was far away, he now goes out to the older son who is standing outside in anger. The father’s love is not reserved for only one of his sons; he pursues both. He will not simply accept the older son’s sulk — he actively goes to him and tries to draw him in.
elements.questionHint: The father left the party to go to the older son — just as he ran to the younger son — what does this pattern of the father always going out tell you about God’s character?

elements.passageText: <sup>29</sup>But he answered his father, ‘Look! These many years I have served you, and I have never disobeyed your commandment, yet you never gave me a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. <sup>30</sup>But when this son of yours came back, who has devoured your assets with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!’

elements.question: How does the older son respond to his father’s initiative?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: He responds with resentment and a transactional view of his relationship with his father: he has served him for years without disobedience, yet was never rewarded with even a small celebration. He frames everything as a business ledger — his loyal service deserved a return that he never received, while his wasteful brother gets the best. He even refuses to call the younger son his brother, calling him ’this son of yours’. His complaint reveals that he never understood the relationship as one of love at all.
elements.questionHint:
Notice that the older son says he ’served’ his father and ’never disobeyed a commandment’.
Does that sound like the language of a son, or of an employee?
What does his choice of words reveal about how he understood his relationship with his father?

elements.passageText: <sup>31</sup>’My child,‘ the father said to him, ‘you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. <sup>32</sup>But we had to celebrate and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again, and was lost and is found!’

elements.question: What is the key point that his father makes in reply?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The father makes two key points. First, the older son has always had everything — ‘you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.’ He was never in a transactional relationship; he was already the heir, in constant companionship with his father. He had missed that entirely. Second, the rejoicing was not optional — it was necessary (‘we had to celebrate’), because a dead person had come back to life. The father also pointedly says ’this brother of yours’, gently correcting the older son’s refusal to own the relationship.
elements.questionHint: The father says ’you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours’ — given that the older son felt deprived and unrewarded, what does this reveal about what he had failed to see or appreciate all along?

elements.text: The older son doesn’t understand his father. He thinks he has to earn his love. He has done a far better job than his brother and he can’t understand why his father wants anything to do with him. He thinks his relationship with his father is based on reward, not love. He is miles from his father, just as lost as his brother ever was. That’s the shock. If you only knew the start of the story, you would have expected the older son to be in the party and the younger one to be outside. The original audience would have got the message loud and clear: ‘be careful you don’t spend big effort on religion, yet without ever knowing God at all’. Jesus has another listening audience in mind. Us! It forces each of us to ask, ‘Where am I in this story?’

elements.question: Ask yourself: Am I more like the younger son, or the older one?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Your thoughts...

elements.question: Am I ’inside the party’ or ’outside’? Have I come home to God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Your thoughts...

elements.text: People often think Christianity is a reward system. Imagine a multi-story building. At the top you have the ’holy’ people (saints, pastors and so on). After that come all the good people (nurses, doctors and so on). Then you get normal people. And right at the bottom you have the murderers, thieves, rapists, and terrorists. The idea is that, at the end of time, God will draw a horizontal line somewhere; probably a little bit below where we are. If you are above the line, you go to heaven; if you are below the line, you go to hell. That’s a common idea, but it doesn’t work like that at all.

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup>he saved us not by works of righteousness that we have done but on the basis of his mercy, through the washing of the new birth and the renewing of the Holy Spirit,

elements.question: How does the Bible contradict that ’tower block’ analogy?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says explicitly that God saved us not because of righteous works we have done, but on the basis of his mercy. The tower block idea assumes that enough good deeds will eventually earn God’s acceptance — but Paul rules that out entirely. Salvation has nothing to do with where we rank on any scale of human goodness; it is entirely a gift of mercy, worked through the new birth and the renewing of the Holy Spirit.
elements.questionHint:
Paul says God saved us ’not by’ one thing but ’on the basis of’ another.
Can you identify both?
How does that distinction demolish the idea of a moral ranking system?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup>yet we know that no one is justified by the works of the law but by the faithfulness of Jesus Christ. And we have come to believe in Christ Jesus, so that we may be justified by the faithfulness of Christ and not by the works of the law, because by the works of the law no one will be justified.

elements.question: How else does the Bible contradict that ’tower block’ analogy?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul is emphatic and threefold in his denial: no one is justified by works of the law — not partly, not mainly, not at all. Justification comes entirely through the faithfulness of Christ, received by faith in him. The tower block model imagines that law-keeping accumulates merit; Paul says that model produces nothing. Whatever floor of the tower block you occupy, your good deeds cannot justify you before God.
elements.questionHint:
Paul repeats the same negative point three times in this single verse.
Why do you think he emphasises it so strongly?
What is he trying to rule out completely?

elements.text: God doesn’t draw a horizontal line. God cuts the tower block vertically. Some at the bottom will spend eternity with Him; some at the top will be shut out. Christianity isn’t about religion, rules, or respectability — it’s about relationship, about knowing God through Jesus. If it were about rules, none of us would get in. God’s standards are far above the top of our building. We can’t enter on our own. God offers to take us back anyway.
God Calls Us Home to Himself
In Luke 15 God paints us a picture of His love. His message to us is one of massive welcome: ‘Wherever you are, whatever you’ve done, come home.’

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup>By this the love of God is revealed in us: that God has sent his one and only Son into the world so that we may live through him. <sup>10</sup>In this is love: not that we have loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the atoning sacrifice for our sins.

elements.question: How can we know for sure that God loves us?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John points to a concrete, historical event as the proof: God sent his one and only Son into the world so that we might live through him. And crucially, the initiative was entirely God’s — not that we loved God, but that he loved us first and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice. The love of God is not a feeling or a claim; it is demonstrated in the most costly act imaginable.
elements.questionHint:
John says that love is shown by who acted first.
Who made the first move in this relationship, God or us?
What did that first move cost?

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup>Who is a God like you, forgiving iniquity and passing over the rebellion of the remnant of his inheritance? He does not remain angry forever, but he delights in loyal love. <sup>19</sup>He will once again have compassion on us; he will subdue our iniquities. You will throw all our sins into the depths of the sea.

elements.question: How else can we know for sure that God loves us?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Micah describes a God who is unique in his forgiveness — who does not hold onto anger forever but who delights in loyal love. He will have compassion, subdue our sins, and throw them into the depths of the sea, never to be retrieved. This is not reluctant tolerance but active, joyful love — a God who takes pleasure in showing mercy. The completeness of the forgiveness (all our sins, into the sea) is a powerful assurance of his love.
elements.questionHint:
Micah says God ’delights in loyal love’ — the word ’delights’ means he takes pleasure in it.
What does that tell you about whether God’s forgiveness is reluctant or wholehearted?

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup>’Come now, let us reason,‘ says the Lord. ’Though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they are as red as crimson, they shall be like wool.’

elements.question: How can we know that God will accept us back, no matter what?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God himself invites the conversation and makes the offer: sins that are as scarlet — deeply stained, seemingly permanent — will be made as white as snow. The contrast is total: from the deepest red to the purest white. God is not saying that our sins are minor or that they don’t matter; he is saying that no stain is beyond his power to remove. The offer is made to people whose sins are real and serious, and the promise is complete cleansing.
elements.questionHint: Scarlet and crimson were colours that couldn’t be removed by washing in the ancient world — so why does God choose these specific colours to describe sins he promises to make white as snow?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup>But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous, forgiving us our sins and cleansing us from all unrighteousness.

elements.question: How else can we know that God will accept us back, no matter what?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John grounds God’s acceptance in his character: he is faithful and righteous, and therefore when we confess, he will forgive and cleanse. This is not a conditional offer that might not hold — it rests on who God is. The forgiveness covers our sins; the cleansing covers ’all unrighteousness’, which is broader still. The one condition on our side is honest confession; everything else is guaranteed by God’s own faithfulness.
elements.questionHint:
John says God forgives because he is ’faithful and righteous’ — rather than saying God forgives because he feels like it.
Why does basing forgiveness on God’s character make the promise more reliable?

blocks.title: Christians who want to grow
blocks.body: If you are already a Christian but feel like your growth has stalled — or if you simply want to grow more — this study is for you. It works through what the Bible says about growing in Jesus: what holds us back, how grace works, and how to get moving again. The goal is not guilt, but growth.

blocks.title: New Christians
blocks.body: If you have recently come to faith, this study will help you get your Christian life off to a strong start. It covers the foundations: repentance and faith, the battle with sin, knowing Christ, and resting in the Father’s love. Working through it carefully will give you something solid to build on.

blocks.title: People exploring Christianity
blocks.body: If you are not yet a Christian but are genuinely curious — wondering what the Christian life actually involves, what it demands, and what it offers — this study is for you too. It doesn’t assume you’ve already made up your mind. It works through what the Bible says and invites you to think carefully about it.

blocks.title: People discipling others
blocks.body: If you are walking alongside someone else in their faith — as a mentor, a small group leader, or a friend — this study gives you a structured way to work through the essentials of spiritual growth together. The seven chapters cover the ground that matters most: what growth looks like, what sin does to us, and what the Father’s love makes possible.

blocks.title: On your own
blocks.body: This study works well as a personal study. Work through each chapter at your own pace, read the Bible passages, write your answers to the questions, and meditate on the reflection questions at the end. There is no right speed — some chapters may take twenty minutes, others may take longer if a question stops you in your tracks.

blocks.title: In a group
blocks.body: The study also works well in a small group setting. You could work through each chapter together from scratch, reading the passages and discussing the questions as a group. Alternatively — and this is often the most rewarding approach — each person works through the chapter individually first, writes their answers, and then the group comes together to discuss what they found. Either way works. The questions are designed to prompt genuine reflection, not just right answers.

blocks.title: Working with a leader or mentor
blocks.body:
It can make a real difference to have someone guiding you through the study — a group leader, a pastor, or a more experienced Christian who can help you think through your answers and questions. Perhaps they are the one who recommended this study to you in the first place.

At the end of each chapter, the Share button lets you send your written answers directly to your leader or mentor — via WhatsApp, email, or any other app on your phone. This gives them a window into your thinking before you meet, and makes for much richer conversation.

blocks.title: Two kinds of questions
blocks.body: Each chapter has two kinds of questions. The Bible questions are tied to specific passages — asking you to look carefully at what the text says. The reflection questions at the end are more personal — asking what the chapter means for you specifically.

blocks.title: Common Misunderstanding boxes
blocks.body: Throughout the study you will encounter darker-coloured cards headed Common Misunderstanding. These address words — like grace, repentance, or faith — that Christians use all the time but that are often misunderstood. Take a moment to think about what you understand by the word, then tap Find out to see a short clarification.

leadersNotesData.subtitle: Grow in Christ
intro: These notes are designed to help group leaders and mentors get the most out of each chapter – both for the people they are leading and for themselves. They are not a substitute for working through the material yourself first. The best leaders are those who have worked through the questions personally before they help others doing the same.

Create a safe space for honesty. The questions in this study are designed to prompt real reflection, not just correct answers. Your job is to make the group feel safe enough to say what they actually think, not what they think a Christian is supposed to say.
Don’t rush the silences. Some of the best moments in a group study happen after a question lands and nobody speaks for a few seconds. Resist the urge to fill every silence.
Watch for the person who goes quiet. Sometimes the most significant thing happening in the room is with the person who says the least. Check in with them afterwards.

keyPoints.body:
This opening chapter establishes the framework for the whole study: the Christian life begins and continues with repentance and faith. Neither can be left behind.

The ’Growth Graph’ concept is central. Use it to get the group to locate themselves honestly — are they on a Graph 3 trajectory (uneven but growing) or a Graph 4 (stalled)? This is not a trick question; the honest answer is the useful one.

Draw out the link between sin and darkness (1 John 1:5–7): the things we keep hidden tend to grow. Repentance is not just a one-off act at conversion — it is the ongoing posture of the Christian life.

pastorals.body:
Some people in the group may feel stuck and ashamed about it. The chapter’s tone is not condemnatory — it is hopeful. Graph 4 can become Graph 5. Make sure that message lands clearly.

Others may be tempted to tick ’Graph 3’ automatically without real reflection. Encourage honest self-assessment; the growth graph exercise only works if people engage with it genuinely.

Watch for people who are embarrassed about ongoing sin (1 John 1:8–9). The chapter addresses this directly: pretending we have no struggles breeds hypocrisy and stalls growth. Help the group see that acknowledging sin to God — and to safe others — is the path forward, not a sign of failure.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who equate spiritual maturity with having fewer struggles. The chapter argues the opposite: mature Christians are more honest about their struggles, not less.

keyPoints.body:
This chapter explores what it means to grow in Jesus: in obedience, in grace, and in knowledge of Christ. These three are not alternatives — they belong together.

The septic tank illustration is deliberately provocative. Use it to press the question: do we actually want to be saved from sin, or just from its consequences? Salvation and discipleship must go together (Matthew 28:19–20).

The section on grace and godliness (Titus 2:12; Romans 5:6–8, 10) is theologically important. Christ didn’t save us because we learned to obey Him. We obey because He has already saved us. This ordering matters enormously for how people approach the Christian life.

pastorals.body:
Paul’s story at the start will resonate with many in the group — the cooling-off pattern is very common. Normalise it, but don’t leave it there: the point is that it doesn’t have to stay that way.

Some may struggle with the idea that God’s love doesn’t depend on their performance. This is deeply counter-intuitive for many people. Take time with Romans 5:6–8 — Christ died for us while we were still sinners, not once we had sorted ourselves out.

The Heart Check Likert scale at the end is designed to surface honest self-awareness. Encourage people to answer it privately and truthfully before any group discussion.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who hear ’grace’ and conclude that obedience doesn’t matter. The chapter is clear that grace produces godliness (Titus 2:12), not a licence to coast.

keyPoints.body:
This chapter presses the distinction between ageing and maturing. Time passes automatically; growth does not. Some people have been Christians for decades and are still stuck at an early stage of maturity — and that is not what God intends.

The passages from Colossians, Psalm 1, and Mark 4 together build a picture of what roots look like in practice: staying rooted in Christ (Col 2:6–7), meditating on God’s Word (Ps 1:2–3), and not allowing the thorns of life to choke growth (Mark 4:7).

The Gospel-Growth Plan section is the practical centrepiece of the chapter. It asks people to identify one specific, personal growth area — not a vague aspiration but a concrete target. This is worth significant discussion time.

pastorals.body:
People may find it uncomfortable to be asked to name a specific growth area. Some will default to something safe and general. Gently push for something real — the exercise only has value if it’s honest.

Be sensitive to the fact that some growth areas (addiction, secret sin, relationship breakdown) may be deeply painful to acknowledge, even privately. The app format gives people privacy; use that as a feature, not a limitation.

The amazing destiny passage (Philippians 3:20–21) is meant to be genuinely motivating. Don’t rush past it — growth is not mere duty; it is moving towards something glorious.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who choose a Gospel-growth area that is really about someone else (‘my marriage’, ‘my family’). The plan should be personal and individual.

keyPoints.body:
This chapter introduces sin as a predator. John Owen’s quote — ‘Be killing sin or it will be killing you’ — frames everything that follows. Sin is not a minor inconvenience; it is actively destructive.

The study of Genesis 3 repays careful attention. The serpent’s tactics — questioning God’s word, distorting His commands, promising what He hasn’t promised — are still in use today. Help the group see how these tactics work in their own experience of temptation.

The section on sin spreading (Genesis 4) shows how quickly sin escalates: from one act of disobedience to fratricide within a generation. The weed-seed illustration makes the point well — small sins are not harmless; they grow.

pastorals.body:
Thomas’s story at the start is deliberately confronting. Some in the group may have their own version of it. The aim is not to shock, but to be honest that sin’s effects can be devastating — and that there is a way back.

The question ’In your life, who is doing better at killing who?’ is intentionally direct. Give people space to sit with that question before moving on. Silence here is often productive.

Watch for people who minimise their sin by comparing it to others’. The half-truth dynamic (Genesis 3) is worth pressing: the most dangerous lies have some truth mixed in.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who have carried hidden sin for a long time and may feel that their situation is beyond hope. The hints of grace in Genesis 3:15 and 3:21 are there for a reason — God has not given up on His purposes of blessing.

keyPoints.body:
This chapter explores sin as refusal — refusal of God’s knowledge, His authority, His goodness, and ultimately of God Himself. Reinhold Niebuhr’s opening quote frames sin as the refusal to accept our creaturely limits.

The sequence of passages builds a cumulative picture of what sin refuses: knowledge (Romans 1:18–23), God’s authority (Romans 5:14; Ezekiel 2:3–5), gratitude (Romans 1:21b), relationship (Leviticus 26:40), and finally God Himself (Romans 1:25).

The contrast with Mark 12:30 is important: the opposite of refusing God is loving Him with everything. Use this to move the discussion from diagnosis to aspiration.

The closing bridge text on sin hierarchies is worth dwelling on — Christians often tolerate invisible sins (pride, greed, envy) while policing visible ones. Jesus didn’t operate that way.

pastorals.body:
This chapter is theologically dense. Don’t feel you need to cover every passage in a group setting — pick the two or three that are most relevant to where your group is.

The question ’Which of these types of refusals are you most at risk of?’ is very personal. It may produce either very honest answers or very guarded ones. Either response is revealing.

The Pharisee dynamic in the closing bridge (Mark 2:15–17) is important pastorally: some group members may be very good at external religion while harbouring deep interior refusals. Handle with care.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who identify easily with the ’refusal of authority’ examples but are blind to their own refusal of gratitude or relationship with God. Both are forms of the same thing.

keyPoints.body:
This chapter turns from the diagnosis of sin to the Father’s love. The parable of the lost son (Luke 15:11–32) is the primary text, explored through the lens of its three main characters.

The younger son represents the person who has walked away from God openly. His journey — from demanding his inheritance to feeding pigs to ’coming to his senses’ — maps onto many people’s experience of sin and its consequences.

The father’s response is the theological heart of the chapter: he sees his son ’while he was still a long way off’, runs to him, and restores him fully. This is not a grudging acceptance — it is extravagant welcome. The robe, the ring, the fattened calf: full restoration, not probation.

The bipolar Likert scale at the start — measuring how the group perceives God’s attitude towards them — sets up a before/after comparison with chapter 7. It’s worth completing carefully.

pastorals.body:
Some in the group will identify painfully with the younger son. Be ready for that. The chapter’s message is one of hope: the father hasn’t given up, and neither has God.

The distinction between leaving through the ’front door’ and leaving through the ’back door’ is pastorally significant. Some people in church settings have never actually come home to God — they’ve just stayed in the vicinity. Handle this gently but honestly.

The question ’Do you mostly feel at home with God, or more distant?’ is a key pastoral barometer. Don’t rush past it.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who have a deeply negative view of God — as distant, judgmental, or indifferent. The parable is specifically designed to correct that picture. Let it do its work.

keyPoints.body:
This chapter completes the parable by focusing on the older son and the listening audience. Jesus originally told the parable to the Pharisees — people who were religious but distant from God in a different way.

The older son’s problem is not irreligion but a transactional view of his relationship with the father. He thinks he has earned love through obedience. He is miles from his father emotionally even while living in his house. This is a searching challenge for churchgoing people.

The ’tower block’ illustration challenges the common assumption that salvation is about being good enough. Titus 3:5 and Galatians 2:16 make clear that no one is justified by works — God cuts the building vertically, not horizontally.

The repeated bipolar Likert scale at the end allows people to compare their perception of God’s attitude towards them before and after engaging with the parable. This can be a powerful moment of reflection.

pastorals.body:
The older son dynamic is often harder to surface in a group than the younger son dynamic. People who identify with the older son are often high-functioning, respectable, and resistant to the idea that they might be ’outside the party’.

The questions ’Am I more like the younger son or the older one?’ and ’Am I inside the party or outside?’ are the most important in the chapter. Give them real time and real space.

The closing comparison of the two Likert scales (from chapters 6 and 7) is an opportunity for a genuinely moving moment — if people have engaged honestly, they may find that the parable has shifted something in how they see God. Be attentive to that.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who give intellectual assent to the gospel (‘yes, I know God loves me’) without any emotional reality to it. The parable is designed to move people, not just inform them.

introduction.body:
This introduction goes with Study 1.

As you start reading this book I want to remind you that the Christian life is a life of repentance and faith. That’s how it starts – with the call to ‘repent and believe the good news!’ (Mark 1:15) – and that’s how it should continue. As Christians we are generally fairly good at continuing with faith – we don’t think faith is something we should leave behind. But we can be more embarrassed about repentance. Maybe we wouldn’t say it out loud, but we can start to think that repentance is something we move on from – that it is for the start of the Christian life, and that mature believers grow out of it.

That’s not true.

When we think about it properly, we know it’s not true, but sometimes we act as if it was true. Christians who have followed Jesus for many years can be embarrassed – and so unwilling – to admit that there is anything they need to repent of. It can feel safe to admit sin in general (‘We are all sinners in need of grace’), but not in particular (‘I still struggle with bad temper, or lust, or pride, or jealousy …’). Leaders can feel the same, and sometimes their followers do not want to hear them admit it, or give them permission to. And admitting sin is not the end of it: we still need to put things right, and to accept correction.

Those attitudes breed hypocrisy – pretending there are no problems when, of course, there will be. Pretending leads us to ignore problems, or to cover them up. Then the problems are not dealt with, and our growth stalls. We are set up for a fall. Sin loves darkness. When you keep it in the dark, it grows.

It shouldn’t be like that. Repentance and faith start the Christian life, and repentance and faith continue the Christian life. When we repent and believe, we turn from sin and we turn to Jesus – the two things go together. They go together at the start of the Christian race, in the middle, and all the way to the end. So as you read this book, I want to encourage you to be serious about faith in Jesus, and to be serious about repentance from sin.

whatDoesYourGrowthGraphLookLike.header: What Does Your Growth Graph Look Like?
whatDoesYourGrowthGraphLookLike.body:
If you are not growing over time, it is right to ask whether something is wrong. Ask yourself a hard question: have I turned from sin and turned to Christ? If you have not, that may be why you are not growing. If you have turned to him and still are not growing, there may be other reasons, and other questions to ask.

Consider the following graphs. In each graph, time runs from left to right. The line is a rough picture of how far you have grown in Christ at each point in time.

The first graph shows a beautifully smooth growth path. Maybe your physical height would grow like this, always increasing nicely until it arrives at a mature, stable level. Christian growth isn’t like this at all. There are successes and there are setbacks, there are ups and there are downs. Real life is never so plain and uniform.

graphTwoText.body: Even Graph 2 is unrealistically predictable. It has its ups and downs but they are modest, and they are neatly managed. The ‘setbacks’ in this graph are almost elegant – small, neat, predictable, and respectable. Real life is messier, more confusing and less predictable.

graphThreeText.body: Graph 3 looks more like a ‘normal’ experience of Christian growth. There is growth, over time, but it is not necessarily smooth, not necessarily elegant, not necessarily pretty. There are advances, and there are setbacks, encouragements and disappointments. If you look at things on a short timescale you can’t always tell whether they are improving or not. But looked at over a longer timescale, you may begin to see what the Holy Spirit has been doing in someone’s life. This is fine and normal and good.

graphFourText.body: But sometimes we end up with something more like Graph 4. For the person in Graph 4, there was spiritual growth for a while, but then somewhere something went wrong. Maybe they can identify the moment when it all started to go wrong, or maybe they can’t. But looking back, it’s obvious something has happened. Their growth has stalled, and they may even have gone backwards. They may not know why.

graphFiveText.body:
As you read this book, I hope you will be able to identify with Graph 3. If so, I hope this book will encourage you to keep going on the path you are already on, and to grow stronger on it. But you may be closer to Graph 4, with your growth stalled or going backwards. My prayer is that, as you read on and talk about what you are learning, God will use this book to give you a chance to change course.

God wants all his children to grow in Jesus. He wants you to grow in Jesus. If you have stalled in your growth, it doesn’t have to stay that way; in fact, it shouldn’t stay that way. Your growth can be restarted. If you fix your eyes again on Jesus Christ, he will help you begin again. Graph 5 shows one way this can happen: the same life as Graph 4, with growth that stalled and then began again. Graph 4 can turn into Graph 5.

aboutTheBook.body:
This book has fourteen chapters. Chapter 1 asks what it means to grow in Christ. After that, the chapters come in pairs: something that holds us back, and then something God gives us so that we can grow. The things that hold us back are sin, shame, idols, wrong motives, bitterness and sexual sin. The gifts are the Father’s love, the gospel, wisdom, grace, repentance and confession, and friendship. Chapter 14 looks back over the whole book, and forward to passing on what we have received. Each chapter ends with some key points, something to put into practice, and questions for reflection. You can read it on your own, but it helps to talk about it with someone you trust. Each chapter goes with a study in this app, so you can use the two together, alone or in a group.

Chapter 1 begins with Paul’s story, which looks like Graph 4. Which graph is nearest to yours now? Draw it, or make a note of it, and keep it: we come back to the graphs in Chapter 14. You can draw your own growth graph in Study 1.
