introduction.body:
[[fn:1]]This chapter goes with Studies 2 and 3.

‘And we all, who with unveiled faces contemplate the Lord’s glory, are being transformed into his image with ever-increasing glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit.’ (2 Corinthians 3:18)

Listen to Paul’s story:[[fn:2]]

I was still at school when I first put my faith in Jesus Christ. I was glad to seize the chance to be accepted by Jesus and to have my sins forgiven. Coming to Jesus was a great experience. Life stopped being just about obeying rules; I learned the joy of allowing God’s Spirit to help me glorify God in my life. And the gospel was such good news to me that I just wanted to make it known to others. I loved following Jesus. But after a while things started to cool down. After school I wanted to get a lucrative job and settle down. My passion for sharing Jesus reduced. There were sins I was still struggling with – I began to wonder if I would ever be free of them. I had grown really quickly in my first few years as a Christian, but then the growth seemed to slow down. I wondered if it was going to stop altogether. I didn’t know what had gone wrong, and I didn’t know how to put it right.

Paul’s story is common. In the introduction it was Graph 4: growth for a while, then a stall. But it’s not the way things should be. It is not enough just to come to Christ. He wants you to grow in him. You should want to grow in him. If you do not want to grow in Christ – if that is your settled choice, and not just tiredness after too much pressure – ask yourself whether you really want to belong to him. Maybe you recognise a time in your life when you felt like Paul; maybe you feel like that right now.

Jesus does not want that to be your experience, and it doesn’t need to be your experience – not over the long run, certainly. So in this chapter we are going to look at what it means to grow in Jesus; and we’ll start with something practical – obedience.

growthAndObedienceToJesus.body:
Suppose your friend had fallen into a septic tank, and he was drowning in it. He calls out, ‘Help! Help! Save me!’ So you reach down and take his hand, and you pull and pull, and eventually you get him out. He says, ‘Thank you very much,’ and he sits on the ground and gets his breath back. And then once he’s recovered, he stands up, and jumps back into the septic tank, and starts drowning again. He calls for help again – ‘Help! Help! Save me!’ – so you reach down again and take his hand again, and you pull and pull, and eventually you get him out. He says, ‘Thank you very much,’ and he sits on the ground again and gets his breath back. And then he jumps back in. And starts to drown all over again.

How many times are you going to pull him out? (Seven times? Seventy-seven times?) Perhaps that depends on how kind and patient you are. So let me ask this instead: How many times will you have to pull him out before you start to suspect he isn’t really all that serious about being ‘saved’ from the tank?

Not many. He can’t be saved from the tank, if he really wants to be back in the tank. And it’s true the other way round as well: if he really wants to be back in the tank, then he doesn’t really want to be saved from the tank. It’s a bit like that with us and Jesus and sin. Jesus calls us to come to him for salvation – to be saved from sin and guilt and shame and wrath and judgment – but we can’t find salvation in Jesus, if we don’t really want to be saved from those things that hold us captive. This is not about someone who falls and gets up again. Christians fall, and some fall many times. The question is whether we keep turning back to Jesus for help, or decide to make peace with our sin. That’s why salvation and discipleship have to go together. That’s why Jesus doesn’t come only to call ‘converts’ but to make disciples. That’s why the Great Commission is a discipleship-commission, not only a conversion-commission:

Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you. (Matthew 28:19-20, emphasis added)

Jesus is very clear about what it means to be his disciple: we are to obey everything he has commanded. That’s strong – but it’s part of what it means to love God and to love Jesus. Just before his crucifixion, Jesus explains the same thing to his disciples:

My command is this: love each other as I have loved you. Greater love has no one than this: to lay down one’s life for one’s friends. You are my friends if you do what I command. I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know his master’s business. Instead, I have called you friends, for everything that I learned from my Father I have made known to you. (John 15:12-15, emphasis added)

Jesus calls us his friends. But it is a unique sort of friendship. It’s not just the same as being friends with someone you grew up with. To be friends with the Lord of the universe is a great privilege – but it doesn’t stop Jesus from being the Lord of the universe. To be his friends means to do what he commands. It means we will learn to grow in obedience.

growthAndChristsGrace.body:
But growing in obedience is not the only thing, and not even the primary thing. If we ask the New Testament what it means to grow as a Christian, one of the answers it gives is this:

But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. (2 Peter 3:18)

There are two things mentioned there – grace, and knowledge – and we will look at them in turn. So first: what does growing in ‘the grace of our Lord Jesus’ mean? Part of what it means is that we grow in our understanding of grace – our understanding that we are accepted freely by God. We do not earn his acceptance by doing well. Yes, obedience has its place – and it’s an important place – but it’s not the foundation. Our acceptance by God depends on Christ alone. God loves you, and he won’t stop. His love does not rise when you do well and fall when you do badly. It rests on what Jesus has already done for you. The apostle Paul says it this way:

You see, at just the right time, when we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly. (Romans 5:6)

That timing is important. It is not that we learned to obey Christ, and then, because of that, he comes to save us. Not at all. It is the other way round. Christ has already come to save us, and because of that, we learn to obey him. We love, because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). We serve, because he first served us. We learn to obey, because while we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly. That gives us the confidence to learn and grow and struggle – to try, and perhaps succeed, perhaps fail, and to try again – knowing that our salvation is already secure:

For if, while we were God’s enemies, we were reconciled to him through the death of his Son, how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through his life! (Romans 5:10)

Some people worry that this kind of grace will make us careless about sin. The Bible says the opposite. Grace is what teaches us to say no to ungodliness and yes to self-control and faithfulness (cf. Titus 2:12). The more we see what God has given us, the less we want to go back to what he saved us from. So growing in grace also means living each day by his grace, and letting that grace, and not fear or pride, move us to obey.

growthAndKnowledgeOfChrist.body:
As well as growing in grace, spiritual growth involves growing in knowledge. But, of course, spiritual growth involves more than just knowledge, but it doesn’t involve less than knowledge. You cannot know someone – certainly you cannot know them well – if you don’t know much about them. If you don’t know about a person, you won’t know how to please them. Suppose I want to buy my wife a new dress for her birthday. And suppose I buy her a dress that is far too big, and in colours that she doesn’t like at all. How will she feel? Probably not very pleased. Instead of expressing love and joy in our relationship, and instead of celebrating her birthday and her life, the present actually emphasises that I don’t know her as well as I should, and that I have not bothered to learn. If we are serious about knowing Jesus, we need to know about him. And the way we do that is through his word. In particular, we need to be people who love the Gospels, and who keep coming back to them. Not just the Gospels, of course – all of God’s word, because all of it points to Christ – but especially the Gospels, because they point to Christ especially clearly.

But as well as being pointed to him, and knowing about him, we need to know him – we need to follow him, to trust his lordship, to learn to depend on him. We grow in our relationship with Christ as we put our knowledge about him into practice, and as we trust him because we know him.

growthAndAgeingAndMaturity.body:
Growth is about more than just allowing time to pass. Ageing is automatic; growing is not, and maturing is not. You can get older without growing in maturity. You can get older without growing in wisdom. You can get older without growing in godliness.

A baby is a gift and a joy. But a baby is meant to grow, and parents are glad to see it. Part of the delight is seeing what the child will become.

But some of us get stuck as baby Christians. Tragically stuck. That is not what Jesus wants for us, and it is not what God intends for us. He wants us to be fully mature. Here’s how the apostle Paul expresses it:

[Jesus] is the one we proclaim, admonishing and teaching everyone with all wisdom, so that we may present everyone fully mature in Christ. (Colossians 1:28, emphasis added)

We will not be fully mature until the New Creation. But that does not mean we cannot grow now. Some believers are further on than others, and we can see it. Already, here and now, we are to be growing in maturity. And the apostle Paul reminds us that the route to maturity in Christ is through Christ himself. That is why Paul dedicated himself to proclaiming Christ, making Jesus known, teaching everyone about him.

Our world is full of people trying to sell you secret knowledge: ‘The secret to success!’ or ‘Ten steps to prosperity’ or ‘The trick to fulfilment’. Well, the ‘secret’ to growing in godliness is not a secret – all the glorious riches of God’s power for life and growth and godliness are available to us in Jesus Christ (2 Peter 1:3). Wherever we are starting from, we can certainly become more mature:

So then, just as you received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to live your lives in him, rooted and built up in him, strengthened in the faith as you were taught, and overflowing with thankfulness. (Colossians 2:6-7)

You have received Jesus as Lord, so continue in him. The word used for ‘live your lives’ literally means ‘walk’ – we are to continue walking in Jesus. The images that the apostle Paul uses here – walking, building, rooting – are all slow and steady images. Not the 100m sprint, but the lifelong journey. We are talking about a daily, steady, step-by-step effort, an ongoing progress towards a goal.

To walk with Christ you need to be rooted in him. Think of the parable of the sower (Mark 4) – the seed without roots doesn’t last. Or think of Psalm 1:3 – where the godly person is like a tree planted by streams of water. A tree needs to be well rooted. If a tree is not well-rooted, it will wither in the dry times, and it may get blown over in the stormy times. If you are not rooted in Christ you will not last through the dry times, you will not last through the stormy times. But if you are rooted in him, you have access to all the resources you need.

There are two different things that can go wrong here. Sometimes people have only heard the message of Jesus superficially, and have never been rooted into him at all. A friend once told me about a very dubious ‘conversion experience’ he had as a boy. He and his friends had been playing football, when an ‘evangelist guy’ came over and interrupted their game. He went on and on at them with a gospel presentation. He went on and on for quite some considerable time. Eventually they realised that the quickest way to get him to stop would be to ‘pray the prayer’ he wanted them to pray. So they did – and then they were free to get back to their football game. For years, my friend assumed this meant he had become a Christian, and wondered why he wasn’t growing as a Christian. It wasn’t till much later that he looked back and realised he had never truly turned to Christ at all.

So it is worth asking yourself: Are you rooted in Christ? Have you turned to him? If you haven’t, turn to him now. If you are not sure whether you have, don’t put it off. Talk to a mature Christian you know and trust, such as a pastor or a leader in your church, and do it right away.

The second way things can go wrong is that we start off rooted in Christ, but after a while we begin looking for our security in something else. That’s one of the ways of ending up with a ‘growth graph’ like Graph 4 in the introduction. We drift away from our root; we wander away from our foundation; and then we stall. In a sense, this is the sort of thing that has happened to the Ephesian church, and Jesus himself confronts them about it:

Yet I hold this against you: you have forsaken the love you had at first. Consider how far you have fallen! Repent and do the things you did at first. If you do not repent, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place. (Revelation 2:4-5)

It may also be that some of you who are reading this have fallen into the same problem the Ephesians did. You started off well in your Christian journey. You were rooted in Christ. But along the way, something happened. As you look back you can see that things have slipped away from you. Perhaps you are less eager to follow Jesus than you used to be, and other things have taken first place in your heart. Tiredness, grief and illness can also dry up our feelings, and that is not the same as forsaking Jesus. But if you have drifted from him, don’t leave it like that. You should also talk to someone about it. A mature Christian you know and trust, such as a pastor or a leader in your church, would be a good person to talk to. Jesus takes this seriously: ‘Repent and do the things you did at first. If you do not repent, I will come to you …’ He wants us to listen, and to turn back.

These are not the only reasons why growth can slow. Illness, grief and hard circumstances can play a part too, so do not decide too quickly what is wrong. Look honestly at your own life, and ask someone wise to help you.

And you do not need to stay stuck. It is not what God has in mind for his children. It is not their destiny:

For those God foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters. (Romans 8:29)

This is an amazing destiny! We are being conformed to the image of God’s own Son, Jesus himself. Growing up in Christ is not about how much Bible we know, or how many years we have been in church. It is about becoming more like Jesus – our character becomes more like God the Son, and we bear more of the fruit of the Spirit:

But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. (Galatians 5:22-23)

That is a key part of our destiny in God’s eternal plan. We glorify him as we grow in self-control. We delight him as we grow in love. We honour him as we grow in kindness.

backToPaul.body: Paul said, ‘I didn’t know what had gone wrong, and I didn’t know how to put it right.’ We cannot know everything about his story. But we can say what would help. He needs to know again that Christ accepts him, and that his own performance cannot win or lose that. He needs to turn from sin and turn back to Jesus, as he did at the start. He needs to tell a mature Christian what is happening. And he needs to choose one specific area to grow in. Paul can do these things today. So can you. Graph 4 can still turn into Graph 5.

keyPoints.body:
1. We grow because Christ has already saved us, not to earn his love.
  2. Jesus calls us to be disciples, not only converts: to obey everything he has commanded.
  3. We grow in grace and in knowledge of Christ, knowing about him from the Bible and knowing him by following him.
  4. Growing is more than getting older. God is making us like his Son, and it shows in our character.
  5. We grow by staying rooted in Christ. If our growth has stalled, we turn to him again and make a plan.

beginAPersonalGospelGrowthPlan.body:
God wants us to grow in Jesus. We can and should grow in Jesus. If we fix our eyes on Jesus we will grow in him. That’s the big idea of this chapter. But it’s important to make that big idea specific and concrete. So let me get you to finish this chapter by applying the big idea to the details of your own life. Think of an area of your life where you need to grow – perhaps an area where your obedience is shaky, or your faith is dull, or your repentance is weak. It might be:

  • A missing virtue
    Perhaps one of the fruit of the Spirit that you are lacking in (for example love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control)
  • A sinful emotion or attitude or type of thinking
    (for example bad temper, lust, greed, jealousy)
  • A sinful behaviour
    (for example gossip, lying, stealing, sexual immorality, misusing money, harsh words)

Don’t choose something very general. ‘Growing as a Christian’ is admirable in principle, but vague in practice. ‘Growing in purity and self-control by reducing sexual immorality’ is better, but still a bit vague. ‘Growing in purity and self-control by no longer watching pornography’ is much better. Choose something that is about growing in Christ. Growing in your mathematical ability is, no doubt, a worthy aim in general. But it is not what we are talking about here. Choose something gospel-focused, something about growing in Christ. And make sure it is personal – personal to you. ‘Growing in my marriage’ isn’t just about you – that’s a two-person job, and if you were to commit to it as a couple that would be great (although it is still a bit general). But assuming you are reading this chapter on your own, then you will need to choose an individual growth plan (you cannot change another person, and you are not responsible for their choices) – something like ‘Becoming a more patient husband and father’ would be better. But it needs to fit your context: How do you want to grow as a follower of Jesus?

Take some time and choose a specific area for yourself for personal growth, and write it down specifically:

My personal gospel-growth area:

(Write your answer in a notebook.)

Then take some time to think through how the gospel encourages you to make this change:

  • How does the area where you need growth prevent you from being more like Jesus?
  • What would maturity in this area look like?
  • How does knowing that you are loved by God encourage you to work on growing?
  • Can you think of anything Jesus did or said that is relevant to this?

(Write your answers in a notebook.)

Finally, choose one step you will take this week, and one mature Christian you trust who could help you keep going. Write them in your notebook. Look at your plan again in a month, and see what has changed.

questionsForReflection.body:
1. Which growth graph is nearest to yours now?
  2. Do you find it easier to believe that God accepts you because of Christ, or because of how you have been doing? What makes you think so?
  3. Where is it hardest to obey Jesus at the moment? What is the real reason it is hard?
  4. Is there something you have kept in the dark that you need to bring to Jesus, and to one mature Christian you trust?
  5. Who could pray for you as you work on your growth area?

footnotes.body: John Owen, Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, ch. 2, in The Works of John Owen, ed. William H. Goold, vol. 6 (Edinburgh: Johnstone & Hunter, 1850-53). The sentence in full reads: ‘Do you mortify; do you make it your daily work; be always at it whilst you live; cease not a day from this work; be killing sin or it will be killing you.’ The edition I used has no page numbers, so I cite by chapter.

I owe the Bible’s words for sin, and the order in which this section takes them, to Millard J. Erickson, Christian Theology, 3rd ed. (Grand Rapids: Baker Academic, 2013), 517-28. The idea of sin as aiming at the wrong target is his, and he quotes H. Ryder Smith on it. The point in note 4 about sins that revolt God is his too.
See John D. Zizioulas, Being as Communion: Studies in Personhood and the Church (Crestwood, NY: St Vladimir’s Seminary Press, 1985), 102.
God is revolted by some sins; they are repulsive to him (for example, Deuteronomy 12:31) – and yet he still offers his message of self-sacrificial, divine love to this sin-ridden world.

introduction.body:
This chapter goes with Studies 4 and 5.

‘Sin is crouching at your door; it desires to have you, but you must rule over it.’ (Genesis 4:7)

‘Be killing sin or it will be killing you.’ (John Owen)[[fn:1]]

John Owen’s quote (‘Be killing sin or it will be killing you’) is short and sharp, but very true. If we nurture sins – even little sins – we give them the opportunity to grow up into something that will kill us. This chapter is titled ‘Sin Holds Us Back’, but Owen might well tell us that that is not strong enough. Sin doesn’t just hold us back; it destroys us, it kills us, it ruins us. God agrees. In Genesis 4:7 God pictures sin as a predator, like a lion. It has come to our door. It is crouching there, ready to spring, ready to pounce, ready to devour. Sin desires to have us, it desires to devour us, it desires to consume us. Will we let it? Are we ready for the fight? Will we ‘rule over’ this predator – or will we become prey?

Uche learned about the danger of sin the hard way. He had grown up in church, heavily involved in choir and many other activities, very well respected. Others in his age group looked up to him as a model Christian. But he had a secret. He had fallen into sexual immorality – and not just immorality, but also abortion. Repeatedly. He felt like a fraud. He felt that his Christian life was over, and that his faith was destroyed. Sin had pounced on him, just like a predator, and he did not see any way back.

Uche is a real man. He has given me permission to tell his story, and I have changed some details so that no one can recognise him.

In this chapter we will take a careful look at this predator, so that we can be ready for it: ready to escape it, ready to master it, ready to kill it, so that it is not killing us. This chapter is honest about how serious sin is. But sin is not stronger than Christ. We do not fight it by willpower alone. We turn from sin and turn to him, and he gives us his Spirit to help us.

theFirstSin.body:
Sin loves deception. The serpent (the NIV calls him ‘the snake’) appears unannounced in Genesis 3, and quickly shows that he is a master of deception. He begins, not with an outright lie, but with an insidious question: ‘Did God really say …?’ This lets him imply that God’s commands are unreasonable, without having to say it directly. He then exaggerates the prohibition to make it seem ridiculous: ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden.’

Eve engages with the serpent. With hindsight, perhaps she should have ended the conversation at once (for example by saying, ‘No. And I don’t want to listen to any more nasty suggestions from you. Goodbye!’). Instead Eve tries to correct the serpent – but she corrects him incorrectly! She tells him that they must not eat from the tree in the middle of the garden, or even touch it, or they will die. Things are already going wrong. Eve is adding to God’s command: God never said anything about touching the tree. She has also distorted her view of the middle of the garden. Genesis 2:9 tells us that there were two trees there: ‘the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil’. It seems that Eve’s eye has already passed over the tree she should be paying attention to, and eating from – the tree of life! – and has focused, unhealthily, on the tree she should be avoiding. This is a paradox. You cannot avoid something by staring at it: the more you look at it, the more it fills your mind. If you want to avoid something, you need to fix your eyes on something else.

The serpent sees his opening, and presses forward to take advantage. He advances towards openly contradicting God, and makes three claims: (i) You will not certainly die; (ii) your eyes will be opened; and (iii) you will be like God, knowing good and evil.

Again, in addition to these explicit claims, there are also some implicit claims, floating just under the surface. The serpent is implying that God is holding Adam and Eve back; that God does not have their best interests at heart; that God’s restrictions are not for their good; and their lives will be better if they rise above God’s restrictions, and seize control of their own destiny.

Interestingly, on the surface the serpent’s claims turn out to be ‘true’ – but deep down they turn out to be devastatingly false. By the end of Genesis 3, Adam and Eve are (i) still alive, for now (not ‘certainly dead’); (ii) the ‘eyes of both of them were opened’ – as they become ashamed of their nakedness (verse 7); and (iii) God declares, ‘The man has now become like one of us, knowing good and evil’ (verse 22). The serpent’s points have turned out to be true, but only superficially. The whole thrust of his temptation was to imply that if they seized control of their own destiny, things would become better for them. It turns out the other way round. They move from being at home in the garden to exile outside it; from fellowship with God to exclusion; from honour to shame; from innocence to guilt; from security to fear; from blessing to curse; and from the sphere of life to the sphere of death.

Many of the ‘best’ lies are half-truths – or, at least, partial truths or distorted truths. Half-truths make lies believable. It is difficult to poison someone by getting them to eat 100% pure poison. It is easier to give them wholesome, tasty food with some poison mixed through it. It’s the same with deception. It is easier to get someone to believe a lie if you mix it with a reasonable amount of truth. The truth gives the lie a ‘ring of truth’ that it would otherwise lack. That’s the serpent’s strategy here, and tragically, it works.

Eating from that tree sowed the seed of chaos. At first glance the sin seems small. But the problem was not ‘just’ the eating of forbidden fruit. The problem was that the eating rejected God’s lordship and asserted human independence. By that eating, Adam and Eve claimed the ‘right’ to disregard the God-given boundaries of good and evil built into creation. Instead they claimed the ‘right’ to define their own ‘good’ and their own ‘evil’. This ‘small’ beginning is a deadly beginning, and it quickly bears fruit in violence, pride, murder and faithlessness.

The coming of sin into our world creates a huge tension. On the one hand, God’s glorious holiness requires that sin be banished. Humanity (and creation) cannot be allowed to continue for ever in their fallen condition. This must be ended – and ended justly. On the other hand, God’s glorious love will not allow his good purposes in creation (and for humanity) to be destroyed. Satan cannot be allowed to win.

The solution to that tension, as we know from the rest of the Bible, is salvation. Eventually that will involve Jesus’ incarnation, the cross, his resurrection and his second coming. But those events will take time.

In the meantime, death enters our world. It is certainly a judgment, and it comes as the ‘wages of sin’ (Romans 6:23). But death is also a mercy. God does not let sinners live for ever in a broken world (Genesis 3:22-24), so sin is not allowed to go on for ever. That does not make death good. It is still an enemy, and Christ will destroy it (1 Corinthians 15:26). Genesis 3 does not say what comes after death. The rest of the Bible does.

Our world goes from being a world under blessing to being a world under curse. The curses of Genesis 3:14-19 do not undo the blessings of creation. They are layered on top of them. Even so, there are signs that God has not given up on his purposes of blessing. He banishes Adam and Eve from the garden, but before he does, he clothes them. And in the midst of the curses there is an enigmatic promise of one to come who will crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15). (The Bible’s long expectation of this Serpent-crusher may help to explain its many genealogies.)

sinSpreads.body:
Sin doesn’t sit still. It spreads from Adam and Eve to their children, and from the eating of the fruit (which seems minor, but is deeply rebellious) to murder, all within one generation. The first brother born into our fallen world kills the second.

Even a ‘little’ sin is far from harmless, because it grows. Suppose you find a few tiny seeds of a fast-growing weed in your field. You do not say, ‘They are tiny, so they do not matter.’ You know that in a few weeks they will choke your crops. Sin is like that. It starts small, then it spreads and takes over.

Adam eats the fruit and hides in shame. A generation later Cain kills his brother and tries to cover it up (Genesis 4:9). A few generations after that Lamech kills a man and boasts about it in a poem for his two wives (Genesis 4:23-24).

Sin spreads. Sometimes we think we can play with sin and get away with it. We think we can touch the darkness and then let go. But too late we find that it swallows us whole.

theNatureOfSin.body:
The Bible has many different ways of describing sin,[[fn:2]] but they can be grouped into categories. We will look at them all as variations on refusal – refusing the good that God wants for us, and trying to grasp our own ‘good’ instead (which turns out to be ‘not good’ in the end). These refusals overlap. We separate them to see different sides of sin, not because every sin fits only one. As you read through these refusals, ask yourself which ones you most often fall into.

Refusal of Knowledge

Sometimes we sin because we do not know what is right. We may not be to blame for this. For example, a young child who takes the Lord’s name in vain, or who worships idols, does so because they are learning from their elders. They don’t know any better, and haven’t had any opportunity (yet) to go beyond the teaching of their elders. Other times ignorance may be entirely the fault of the ignorant sinner; for example, a pastor who teaches what he has never checked in the Bible.

Mistakes can be sins too. A driver who takes the wrong road in the dark has made an honest mistake. A driver who was warned that the road was bad, and did not check, has not. Even an honest mistake may need putting right: someone who ate a sacred offering by mistake still had to make restitution (Leviticus 22:14).

We can also be led astray. The Bible warns us, ‘do not let anyone lead you astray’ (1 John 3:7). If we follow a teacher or a friend we have good reason to doubt, we cannot say it was not our fault.

And sometimes we simply do not listen. We hear God’s word and let it pass (Hebrews 2:1-3). This can make us blind to our own sin – and even blind to our blindness.

We can see some of these in Genesis 3. Eve was deceived, and she did not hold on to what God had said.

Refusal of Thankfulness

Sin often involves ingratitude. God is the generous Father of all gifts. He has created a wonderful universe (albeit one that is now broken), and he has blessed his creatures with the gift of life. He has made humans in his own image, for relationship with him. And how has humanity responded? ‘They neither glorified him as God nor gave thanks to him’ (Romans 1:21). We have so much to thank God for. Yet in the ‘good times’ we so often forget to be thankful (not noticing the Giver of what is good), and in the ‘bad times’ we just complain (not noticing the good that we still enjoy, nor the One who is still giving it to us).

Refusal of God’s Authority

A great deal of sin is a conscious refusal of God’s authority. God tells us what he wants, and we do something else. Adam and Eve were given one clear command, and they broke it (Genesis 2:16-17; 3:6). When we sin, we fail to live up to God’s standards of righteousness.

Sin can also be ‘missing the mark’. This is not like an archer whose arrow slips by accident. It is like an archer who aims at the wrong target, and hits it. The target God has set is perfect love for him and for other people. When we fail to love others, we sin against God too (Matthew 22:37-39).

Sin can also be rebellion. Both believers and unbelievers can rebel against God. God told Ezekiel that Israel was a rebellious nation, obstinate and stubborn (Ezekiel 2:3-5). We can be stubborn too, and refuse to give God a hearing.

Refusal of Relationship with God

Sin also damages our relationship with God. We stop respecting him. We turn in on ourselves, and think only about what we want. And we are unfaithful to him (Leviticus 26:40).

Refusal of God’s Goodness

Sin also refuses God’s goodness. We call good things evil and evil things good (Isaiah 5:20). We take what is straight and bend it out of shape. Sin brings confusion, quarrels and disorder, because it is at war with itself (James 4:1-2). God is one, truth is one, and goodness is one. But evil and sin are divided, and they fight against themselves. Sin is both a tragedy and an atrocity.

Refusal of God

Ultimately, sin is our refusal to let God be God. We want to displace him, and replace him with something else. The first commandment reminds us how serious it is to set something else up in place of God (Exodus 20:3; Mark 12:30). Yet it is typical of fallen human behaviour: we exchange God’s truth for a lie, and worship and serve created things rather than the Creator (Romans 1:25). Instead of honouring God, we make our own self the centre of everything.[[fn:3]]

theReachOfSin.body:
Having seen what sin is like, we will now look at its reach: how far does it get? How much of life does it affect?

How Much of Our Lives Does Sin Affect?

Sin reaches into every part of our lives. Think of one drop of ink in a glass of clear water. Stir it, and every part of the water is changed. Sin works like that. It reaches our thoughts, our words, our choices and our desires.

How Deeply Does Sin Affect Us?

But sin does not mark everyone, or every part of a person, in the same way. One drop makes the water a little grey. Add more ink, and it gets darker. Every part of us has been touched by sin, but none of us is as bad as we could be.

Sin is also a state, and not only an act. It affects who we are, and not only what we do.

effectsOfSin.body:
Effects on Our Relationship with God

We shall pick out three ways that sin affects our relationship with God: wrath, judgment and alienation.

Wrath. God is angry at our sin (John 3:36; Romans 1:18). Certainly the Bible’s teaching about God’s wrath can be cruelly distorted, and can be misused to paint a picture of a vindictive God, totally unlike the loving Father of our Lord Jesus. But other times God’s love is sentimentally distorted, to paint a picture of a superficial God who is not especially bothered by evil. It is important to think about all God’s attributes together. God is love, and he is also the God who expresses wrath against evil-doing. God cares enormously about good and truth and beauty; we call this his love. That means he also cares enormously about the destruction of good and truth and beauty; we call this his wrath.[[fn:4]] God’s love and his wrath are connected – to downplay God’s wrath against evil is to downplay his love of the good. There is more to say – for example, God’s wrath is always shaped by his mercy – but we must not say less.

Judgment. God is the Judge of all the earth, and he has entrusted that judgment to his Son (Genesis 18:25; Acts 17:31). From Genesis 1 God has been our loving and generous Creator; from Genesis 3 we also see him acting as our Judge: we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, to give an account of how we have lived (see 2 Corinthians 5:10). And, tragically, we all stand before him as unrighteous people, unable to do his will, moral failures.

Alienation. Our relationship with God is overthrown, and we are estranged from him. Just as Adam and Eve were cast out of the garden, we are separated from God’s presence, and we cannot find our own way back. God is light and holiness, and we have turned to darkness and corruption. And the problem is: light cannot co-exist with darkness, holiness cannot co-exist with corruption; one will drive the other out. As sinners, if we came into God’s presence (without redemption) – if we saw his face without mediation – we would die (see Exodus 33:20). Instead of reacting to God with humility and delight, we react with fear – not the godly fear of deep respect, but the terror of those who know they cannot hide, even when they try to (Revelation 6:15-17; see Genesis 3:10).

Effects on Our Relationship with Other People and the Rest of Creation

Alienation. We were created to love one another. The Fall does not completely obliterate mutual love relationships between people, but it severely disrupts and damages them. Families experience conflict (see Genesis 4:1-16), even close friendships fall apart (see Acts 15:36-40), and people generally distrust or despise one another (see Titus 3:3). We become less able to empathise, less able to see things from other people’s perspective, less able to put their interests first (see Philippians 2:3-5, 20-21). Not that all this always happens to all relationships – God’s common grace (his kindness to all people, whether they believe or not) prevents such a disaster – but it often happens to many, and could in principle happen to any.

Deception and misunderstanding. Sin leads to deception, confusion and misunderstanding. Satan is the father of lies, and deception is his native language (John 8:44). Thankfully human relationships are not always as bad as that, but sadly deception and half-truths all too often mark our interactions.

Conflict. Sin creates conflict. We are all inclined to self-centredness, to putting ourselves first. But that doesn’t work – everybody can’t be first, not all at the same time. And when we try it, conflict becomes inevitable (see James 3:16). Sin puts everything out of joint; we cannot be at peace with one another when we are not at peace with God. We are not even at peace within ourselves – our sinful desires are not unified and consistent – they are at war with one another (see James 4:1-2), so it is no surprise when that internal war spills out into our relationships.

Exploitation. From Genesis 3 onwards, we have turned our backs on the stewardship we were called to. We were given dominion over creation in the model of God’s dominion – caring, loving, and good. Too often we have followed a pattern of dominion modelled more on Satan’s characteristics: exploitative, devouring, consuming. We exploit other people, and we exploit creation itself. Too often the rich exploit the poor; the strong exploit the weak; the cunning exploit the naive. ‘Slavery’ in one form may have been abolished, only for ‘human trafficking’ to re-emerge.

Effects on Our Self

Self-deception and self-misunderstanding. God has built order into the universe, including moral order. The Fall does not destroy that order, but it does fracture and obscure it – it distorts both reality itself, and also our knowledge of reality. Often we will be in denial about our sin, pretending to ourselves that it doesn’t exist, and doing our best to ignore its consequences.

Further corruption. We have exchanged purity for a downward spiral of corruption. The more we give in to sin the further it takes us away from what we were created to be; the further it takes us from what it means to be truly human (the model for which we see in Christ).

sinAndDiscipleship.body:
We Are Born into Sin

Some sins we are born into. We wake up in a world we did not choose, and it is already marked by sin. Tribalism is an example. A child learns very early which tribe is ‘ours’ and which is ‘theirs’, and whom to trust and whom to fear. No one asked the child. Long before the child can choose, the child has inherited old wrongs: land taken, jobs shared out unfairly, violence between families and tribes. Some of us gain from what our group did to others. Some of us carry bitterness from what others did to our group. In other places the same sin is called racism. Corruption is another example. A young man starting work may find that bribes are ‘how things are done’. He did not start the system, but he is now part of it.

Once we wake up to these things, we can play an active part in whether we make them worse or try to make some kind of repair, whether we deepen the bitterness or work towards forgiveness. How we respond matters greatly, and carries great responsibility. But it does not undo the fact that we start from compromised situations. We are born into a sinful human race, and we share in the advantages and disadvantages of those sinful compromises before we are even aware of it.

Some Sins Are Consciously Chosen

Some sins are consciously chosen. We know they are wrong, and we do them anyway. Many of the big, obvious, outward sins fall into this category: theft, murder, adultery. It is harder to commit these sins by accident. This also applies to less obvious sins such as lust, lying, jealousy and pride, which are also often consciously chosen. And it can apply to the sins we are born into. Think again of tribalism. We are born into it without choice. But having been born into it, people all too often choose to embrace at least some of it. We choose to look down on another tribe. We take the prejudice we inherited and make it our own.

Some Sins Are Insidious

Other sins are insidious. They sneak up on us without our realising it. Often we should have realised it, and are blameworthy for not realising – but part of the sneaky nature of sin is that it makes us blind to our sin. It even makes us blind to our blindness! We can be committing additional, active sins without even noticing. We sin more than we know (see Psalm 19:12-13). Take tribalism again. We can tell jokes about another tribe, pass over a good applicant because of the name on the form, or avoid a neighbour because of the language they speak – and not notice what we are doing.

Christianised ‘Hierarchies’ of Sin

Christians sometimes create for themselves hierarchies of sin that are based not so much on the Bible’s values as on the values of what is respectable in their culture. To this way of thinking, outward and blatant sins are bad, but ‘invisible’ sins are overlooked. Sexual sin (for example adultery and fornication) is ‘bad’, but pride, greed and jealousy are tolerated, overlooked or excused.

But so often we do not discern things as God would (which is understandable, as he knows everything), or even as God would like us to (which is less understandable). God’s judgment takes into account the opportunities that people have had: from those who have been given much, much will be demanded (see Romans 2:12-15; Luke 12:48). It may well be that God will judge an outwardly respectable church leader (who has had every Christian privilege, yet is consumed with pride, unforgiveness and rivalry) more strictly than he will judge a young man whose sins everyone can see (and who has had few Christian privileges).

Jesus did not simply go along with the respectable hierarchies of sin of his day. This was one reason why the Pharisees kept coming into conflict with him, and why the ‘sinners’ were open to his message (see Mark 2:15-17). We would be foolish to line ourselves up with the Pharisees in that argument.

Uche – the young man we began this chapter with, the one who had been ‘pounced’ on by sexual sin – was slow to ask for help, and slow to confess his sin. He knew about these ‘Christian hierarchies’ of sin, and he was afraid of being branded as a modern-day ‘tax collector and sinner’. He was afraid of becoming an outcast. Fortunately his story does not end there. We come back to Uche at the end of this chapter, and you will meet him again in Chapter 4. But his story did get stuck at that point for several discouraging years. Don’t fall into the same trap that he did.

The ‘Mundane’ Matters to God

Everything we do has significance, as it will all be judged by Christ. Most of our lives are mundane – not spectacular, not world-changing, just everyday details and ordinary actions. But God is the God of our everyday details. The small things in our lives have real significance, because Jesus himself will judge them!

No Place for Self-Righteousness

All of us are sinners in need of salvation. Some of us have the joy of already finding that salvation. That may make us more blessed, more ‘given-to’. It does not give us any grounds to be self-righteous.

What about the charge that Christians are hypocrites? If this charge only points to the fact that we don’t live up to our own standards, then it is bound to be true. ‘Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect,’ Jesus tells us (Matthew 5:48), and ‘Love each other as I have loved you’ (John 15:12). If the standard we are aiming at is the perfect love of Christ, then we will always fall short of it. That is the normal Christian life this side of the New Creation. But the charge of ‘Hypocrite!’ often implies a bit more. It often implies that we set high standards and (implicitly or explicitly) claim to meet them, even though we don’t. We should not be hypocrites in this way. Yet sometimes we help to build Christian communities that make this sort of hypocrisy normal, by implying that ‘proper Christians’ don’t need to repent. We might not say this out loud, but the message is that repentance is fine at the beginning of the Christian life, while Christian maturity is about overcoming sin and so leaving repentance behind. This is a mistake, and a recipe for hypocrisy. Repentance is, and should be, a normal, everyday part of the Christian life.

You won’t grow if you don’t repent of your sin. Repentance is how you master the beast crouching at your door, the beast that desires to have you. Turning from sin, and turning to Christ – that is how to kill sin before it kills you.

backToUche.body: Uche’s story did not stay stuck. In the end he asked for help, and the person he told did not turn away from him. What Uche found was not a lighter view of sin. He found a Saviour who had already dealt with it. As Paul says, ‘there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus’ (Romans 8:1). Sin had pounced on Uche. But Christ had already carried his sin and his shame. If you are where Uche was, you do not have to stay there. Tell one person you trust – someone who will listen, and will not shame you. Chapters 4, 11 and 13 say more about how to choose.

keyPoints.body:
1. Sin is a predator crouching at the door. We must master it, or it will master us.
  2. Sin lies. Half-truths make lies believable.
  3. Sin starts small and spreads. No sin is too ‘little’ to matter.
  4. Sin touches every part of us and harms our relationships with God, with other people and with ourselves. We are not as bad as we could be, but no part of us is untouched.
  5. Pride and greed matter as much as the sins people notice. We have no ground for self-righteousness and no need to hide. Every day, turn from sin and turn to Christ, who has carried our sin and shame.

puttingItIntoPractice.body: This week, choose one sin you have been treating as small. Write down what it is, and one way it has begun to grow. The Sin check-up in Study 4 can help you choose. Tell God about it in plain words, and ask him to help you turn from it. Then tell one person you trust, chosen as ‘Choose Carefully’ in Chapter 11 describes. If you do not know whom to trust, begin with a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor you have good reason to trust. This step is for sins you have committed. Being sinned against is not your sin to confess. If you have been abused, or are in danger, see Chapter 10, ‘If You Have Been Abused, or Are in Danger’.

questionsForReflection.body:
1. Where has sin used a half-truth to mislead you? What did it promise, and what did it give?
  2. Think of a sin you once called ‘little’. Has it grown?
  3. Which of the six refusals are you most at risk of: not knowing, not giving thanks, not obeying, not staying faithful to God, not wanting God’s goodness, or not letting God be God?
  4. Which sins does your church or family talk about most, and which does it overlook? Where do you tend to place yourself?
  5. What sin could you turn from today? Are any sins mastering your life now? Who could you turn to for help?

footnotes.body: I first heard this parable taught in this way by Vaughan Roberts at St Ebbe’s Church, Oxford, some time in the 1990s. This chapter follows the shape of the notes I took, including the picture of the tower block, but I have written it in my own words, and any errors are mine.

A well-known printed version is Pete Hamill’s newspaper column ‘Going Home’ (New York Post, October 1971), which he said he had heard by word of mouth. The song, by Irwin Levine and L. Russell Brown, was recorded by Tony Orlando and Dawn in 1973. For the history of the story, see Gerald E. Parsons, ‘How the Yellow Ribbon Became a National Folk Symbol’, Folklife Center News (Library of Congress) 13, no. 3 (Summer 1991): 9-11.

introduction.body:
[[fn:1]]This chapter goes with Studies 6 and 7.

‘But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms round him and kissed him.’ (Luke 15:20)

There’s a story, told in many versions, that became a song in America in 1973. The song was called ‘Tie a Yellow Ribbon Round the Ole Oak Tree.’[[fn:2]] Not everyone liked the song, but the story behind it is great. I have told it here with some Nigerian details. Some students were going for a holiday in Florida, and they were travelling down by coach. There were other people on the coach, but they noticed one man in particular. He sat on his own, at the back. He didn’t talk to anyone. Whenever the coach stopped everyone got off to stretch their legs, except for him. He just sat on his own. Eventually one of the students decided that he would try to talk to him. So when everyone else got off at the next stop, he went to the back of the coach, and sat beside him. ‘We’re students, going on holiday,’ he told him. ‘Where are you going?’

‘I don’t really know,’ he said. ‘I was released from prison yesterday, and this coach will take me through the town where I used to live. My wife still lives there, it’s where we both grew up. After we got married, we bought a house and settled down. But then the finances got a bit tight. We were struggling to get by, so eventually I went to New York to look for work. But I got in with the wrong crowd, and one thing led to another. I got involved in some 419 and I was arrested and sent to prison. It was too far for my wife to come to visit. She did write letters. But a while ago they stopped.

‘Well, I got out of prison yesterday. I’ve written to my wife to tell her that I’ll be coming through town on this coach. I said I’d understand if she didn’t want to have me back. “But if you do want me back,” I said, “then tie a yellow ribbon round the old oak tree at the edge of town. If I see it, then I’ll know you still want me back, and I’ll get off the bus and come home. But if there’s no ribbon on the tree, then I’ll understand. I’ll stay on the bus and just keep going.”’

Once everyone knew the story, the whole atmosphere in the bus changed. As the coach got near the town, the tension mounted and mounted. They got to within a mile or two and everyone was looking and looking, trying to be the first to catch a glimpse of this oak tree. And at last the coach turned a corner, and there the tree was. And there was no yellow ribbon on it. But even so, the whole coach erupted in cheers. You see, the tree was completely covered in yellow wrappers. The prisoner was coming home.

Homecomings can be powerful, moving events. And the passage we are going to look at in this chapter is also about someone coming home: the parable of the lost son.

11 Jesus continued: ‘There was a man who had two sons. 12 The younger one said to his father, “Father, give me my share of the estate.” So he divided his property between them.

13 ‘Not long after that, the younger son got together all he had, set off for a distant country and there squandered his wealth in wild living. 14 After he had spent everything, there was a severe famine in that whole country, and he began to be in need. 15 So he went and hired himself out to a citizen of that country, who sent him to his fields to feed pigs. 16 He longed to fill his stomach with the pods that the pigs were eating, but no one gave him anything.

17 ‘When he came to his senses, he said, “How many of my father’s hired servants have food to spare, and here I am starving to death! 18 I will set out and go back to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. 19 I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.” 20 So he got up and went to his father.

‘But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms round him and kissed him.

21 ‘The son said to him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.”

22 ‘But the father said to his servants, “Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. 23 Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let’s have a feast and celebrate. 24 For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.” So they began to celebrate.

25 ‘Meanwhile, the elder son was in the field. When he came near the house, he heard music and dancing. 26 So he called one of the servants and asked him what was going on. 27 “Your brother has come,” he replied, “and your father has killed the fattened calf because he has him back safe and sound.”

28 ‘The elder brother became angry and refused to go in. So his father went out and pleaded with him. 29 But he answered his father, “Look! All these years I’ve been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. 30 But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!”

31 ‘“My son,” the father said, “you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. 32 But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.”’ (Luke 15:11-32)

theYoungerSon.body:
We will look at three characters who feature in this story. The first of those characters is the younger son. He is an assertive young man. Normally people wait until after someone is dead before they try to claim an inheritance, but this lad doesn’t want to wait. He wants it now so he can be free. So he says to his father, ‘Father, give me my share of the estate.’ That is very demanding, very rude. But it’s worth noticing that his father gives him what he has asked for – he doesn’t force him to stay.

And once he gets his hands on the money, the son jets off to a distant country to have the time of his life. It is like heading off to Lagos. He has a great time making lots of new friends – until, eventually, the money runs out. And then suddenly the friends seem to vanish too. Things aren’t going so well any more. He sinks lower and lower, until he ends up as a pig-feeder. He started off wanting to be free, he ends up enslaved.

And it gets worse – verse 16: ‘He longed to fill his stomach with the pods that the pigs were eating, but no one gave him anything.’ We are supposed to be shocked by that. A Jewish boy feeding pigs – and so hungry he starts to envy them! You can’t get lower than that. It’s a tragic picture. And perhaps as some of you read this, you can identify with this young man. It’s the story of lots of people. God made us, God loves us, but we take it all for granted. We don’t want anything to do with him. He gets in our way. And so in our different ways we leave home. We turn our backs on the God who loves us.

Some of us march out of God’s front door. We make it very clear that we don’t want anything to do with God. ‘I’m going to be my own boss, I’ll do what I want, when I want.’ Others leave more quietly through the back door. If that’s you then you probably still believe in God, and come to church often enough. Maybe you are even very involved in church activities. But when it comes to important things, you do what you want, not what God wants. Perhaps you have not made such a big scene about it, but you are still far away from God, doing your own thing without reference to him.

That’s basically what the word sin means: doing your own thing, forgetting about God, ignoring his standards. Living in his world without paying him any real attention. That doesn’t mean sin always makes you feel unhappy – certainly not straight away. Sin can be fun. We all know that, because we have all enjoyed it. But it’s like an addiction. It’s a very hollow sort of fun. We need more and more and more to satisfy us, and it’s still never enough. In the long term we end up destroying ourselves. We end up in the pig-house. And of course it will be like that when we reject God’s standards. He made us, he knows how we should live. Sin – putting myself at the centre of the universe – always brings with it bitterness, envy, selfishness, arrogance, hatred. We hurt ourselves and we hurt others.

Maybe you have recognised something of the younger son in yourself. Maybe you have run away from God. Maybe you have left home, even though you are not necessarily in the pig-house yet. Well, that’s where this young man is, and it’s there that he comes to his senses. He knows that even his father’s servants are better off than this. So he decides to go back home. But there’s a question that must have troubled him: Will his father have him back, after all that he has done?

Well, he needn’t have worried. It’s time to look at our second character – the loving father.

theLovingFather.body:
Imagine the scene as the boy makes his way home: it must have been an anxious journey for him. And as he is walking along, you can imagine him practising his little speech. ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. … Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you.’ And so on.

Far away, an old man stands on top of a hill. He has been there many times before, scanning the horizon. His friends told him that he should have given up hope long ago, but still he comes, watching and waiting. Then, off in the distance he sees a speck appear. And though his eyes are past their best, love makes them sharp. He watches the speck slowly take on the form of a man – thin, and half-starving. Prematurely old. But despite the scrawny face, the old man recognises him, and he sets off, racing down the hillside. ‘My son!’ he cries, and throws his arms around the boy.

The son thinks it’s speech time so he begins his lines, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you.’ But his father doesn’t let him get any further. It’s not speech-time, it’s party-time. So full of joy, he takes him home and tells his servants to bring out some new clothes. ‘Kill the bull, we’ll have a party. This son of mine was dead, and is alive again, was lost and is found.’ That loving father is a picture of God himself.

Now, most of the time, we only get to know people on the outside. Others don’t really know what you are actually like on the inside. We would be very worried if other people knew all the ins and outs of our lives – everything that we have thought, and said, and done. If we think about it that way, we are perhaps worried that if others really knew us then they would wish they didn’t! And if we are worried about what other fallible humans might think, then we certainly don’t want God to know what we are really like. And the problem is that he does – he knows everything about us. But this story tells us that even though God knows everything about us, he still loves us and wants us back. There hasn’t been a day when God hasn’t thought of us, looking for some sign that we will come home.

God wants us back, and to show his love for us he didn’t tie a yellow ribbon to a tree. He put his Son there. Pinned to a cross. That’s God’s great declaration to the world that he loves us and wants us home. Jesus didn’t deserve to die – we deserve God’s judgment, for all the wrong that we have done and the hurt that we have caused. But he died in our place so that we could come home to God, freely forgiven. That’s God’s offer of love to each of us. A new life that starts with Jesus.

theListeningAudience.body:
So, a lost son and a loving father. Now we come to the final character – characters, I suppose – the listening audience.

If you glance at the start of Luke 15 (Luke 15:1-2) you will see that Jesus was originally aiming this story at religious people. Respectable people who were living a decent enough life, unlike the younger son in this story. They couldn’t understand why Jesus would waste his time on people like that. Well, for religious people the punch of this parable comes with the older son. He is often forgotten, but we find him in verse 25, working out in the fields. No doubt he is a hard worker – the sort who probably goes to church regularly. He hears the party going on and asks one of the servants what’s happening. ‘Your brother has returned and your father is throwing a party.’

When he hears this he is furious, and he refuses to come in. So his father comes out to him to try to convince him to join the party – he loves both his sons. But the boy won’t have any of it: ‘What do you think you’re doing throwing a party for this rascal, after he’s thrown away all your money? I’ve been slaving away for you for years, and you’ve never had a party like this for me!’ Look what his father says in reply:

My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found. (Luke 15:31-32)

The older son doesn’t understand his father at all. He thinks he has to earn his way into his father’s good books. He has done a better job than his brother and he can’t understand why his father wants anything to do with his brother. He thinks his relationship with his father is based on reward, not love. And he is miles away from his father. He is just as lost as his brother ever was. And that’s the shock. If you only knew the start of the story you would have expected the older son to be in the party and the younger one to be outside. I’m sure the original audience would have got the message loud and clear: Be careful you don’t put a lot of effort into religion, yet without ever knowing God at all.

And Jesus has another listening audience in mind. You see, it forces each of us to ask ‘Where am I in this story? Am I more like the younger son, or the older one? Am I inside the party or out? Have I come home to God?’ When it comes to Christianity a lot of people think in terms of a reward system. Imagine a tower block. Right at the top you have all the really holy people – saints and pastors and missionaries. After that come all the really good people – nurses, doctors and so on. Then you get normal people. And right at the bottom you have the murderers, thieves, rapists, and terrorists. And the idea is that at the end of time God will draw a horizontal line somewhere – probably a little bit below where we are. If you are above the line, you go to heaven; and if you are below the line, you go to hell.

That’s a common idea – but it doesn’t work like that at all. It can come as a shock to discover that God doesn’t draw a horizontal line. He cuts the tower block vertically, right down the middle. That means there will be people at the bottom who spend eternity with God, and people at the very top who stay outside the party, left out in the cold. That’s because Christianity isn’t about religion or rules or respectability – it’s about relationship. The crucial question is whether you know God – whether you are in relationship with his Son Jesus Christ. If it was about rules, we would all be shut out. God’s standards are way above the top of our tower block. None of us will get in on our own. But the good news is that God is offering to take us back anyway.

comeHome.body:
One last story. I heard it told as a true one, and I have not been able to trace it. It’s a story about a young girl who left home to go to the big city. She did write home for a while, but soon the letters stopped. Her mother got more and more anxious. She imagined the worst and after a while she couldn’t stand it any more. So she saved up the fare to the city. When she got there she searched all the places where young people end up in the city, trying to find her daughter. But she never did; and eventually she had to go home. Before she went, she had a photograph taken of herself, and had lots of copies made. She went back and pinned one up in each of the places she had visited. And then she got back on the train and went home.

A week later, her daughter was in one of those places, and across the room she suddenly saw a photograph of her mother pinned to the wall. She went over and took it down. And when she turned it over, she found these words written on the back: ‘Wherever you are, whatever you’ve done, come home.’ And it broke her heart. Within hours she was on a train and heading home.

Here, in this story from Luke’s Gospel, God has sent us a picture of his love. And on the back, written, so to speak, in blood, is the same message: ‘Wherever you are, whatever you’ve done, come home.’

This chapter will finish with a prayer, in the grey box below. The prayer won’t be for everyone reading this – many people will have come home to God already, and if that is you, you could thank him for it again. But if you know that you are away from home, and away from God, then this prayer is for you. Maybe your ears pricked up as we looked at one of the sons – maybe the younger son, or maybe the older son. If that is you, if you know you need to come home to God, then let me encourage you to come home today.

prayer.body:
Dear God,
I’m sorry that I’ve ignored and rejected you.
Please forgive me.
I want to come home to you.
Thank you that you still love me.
Please help me live with you as my Father and my God.
Amen

If you have prayed that prayer, thank God. The words are not a magic formula. What matters is that you meant them, and that you are trusting Jesus. Then tell a pastor or a Christian friend you trust.

keyPoints.body:
1. Sin is doing our own thing and forgetting God. We can leave home by the front door or the back. It can be fun for a while, but it ends in the pig-house.
  2. The father in the story is a picture of God. He has been watching for us. He runs to meet us, and he does not wait for our speech.
  3. God did not tie a ribbon to a tree. He gave his Son, who died in our place, so that we can come home freely forgiven.
  4. The older son was as far from his father as the younger one. Religion, rules and respectability cannot earn God’s love.
  5. God invites both kinds of lost son home, wherever they are and whatever they have done.

puttingItIntoPractice.body:
Study 6 and Study 7 use these seven pairs. For each pair, ask which is closer to what you really believe about how God sees you – not what you know you ought to say. Write your answers down.

  1. God accepts me despite my faults – or – God rejects me because of my faults.
  2. God loves me – or – God doesn’t care about me.
  3. God has forgiven me for everything – or – God has not forgiven some things.
  4. God frees me to flourish – or – God restricts me from flourishing.
  5. God directs my life – or – God ignores where my life is going.
  6. God is passionately interested in me – or – God is not interested in me at all.
  7. God looks at me with joy – or – God looks at me with disappointment.

Now read the whole parable (Luke 15:11-32) again, slowly, and answer again. Did anything change? Choose the statement you find hardest to believe, and say it to God this week: ‘Father, I find it hard to believe that …’ Ask him to show you that it is true, and be patient if your feelings take time to catch up. If you find that you believe God rejects you or is disappointed in you, talk to a pastor or a Christian friend you trust. The father in the story ran to meet his son. That is what God is like.

questionsForReflection.body:
1. Which are you more like at the moment, the younger son or the older son? What makes you say so?
  2. Some of us leave God by the front door, and some by the back. Is there any part of your life where you have quietly gone your own way while still coming to church?
  3. When God looks at you, what do you imagine he sees, and what do you imagine he feels? How does the picture of the father running change that?
  4. Have you ever felt that you had squandered something valuable? How did you handle it, and who did you tell?
  5. What would coming home to God mean for you in practice this week, in one area where you are struggling?
